Mr. FINLAY MacDONALD (South Cape Breton) asked leave under rule 39 to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the industrial crisis arising out of the announced intention of the directors of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, Limited, to default in payment of interest on bonds maturing July 1, 1926, with consequent unemployment on a large scale, and distress particularly in the province of Nova Scotia.

I am not quite sure that it is a matter of urgent public importance but of course according to rule 39 if twenty members rise the hon. gentleman may proceed.
The Clerk assistant having stated that more
than twenty members had risen:
Dominion Iron and Steel

I appreciate the responsibility of any hon. member moving the adjournment of the House and in order to do so he must be able to justify himself by calling the attention of the House to a matter of urgent public importance. The subject that I am going to bring to the attention of hon. members this afternoon is one not only of grave, but of vital importance to the people of eastern Canada. For the past few days the financial press of Canada has carried the news that the directors of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, Limited, intend to default in the payment of interest and sinking fund on their bonds, the first issue of which matures on July 1, and the second on September 1. The importance of such a move as this cannot be exaggerated. It is widespread and it is going to have a most disastrous effect as regards not only the island of Cape Breton, but the whole of eastern Canada.
The Dominion Iron and Steel Company, Limited, is one of the constituent companies of the British Empire Steel Corporation. It has been in existence for about a quarter of a century. It was organized about 1899 and began operations two or three years later. It is situated in the city of Sydney which at the time of its inception was a town of 3,500 inhabitants. Owing to the establishment of that company there, the town has grown into a city of about 25,000 inhabitants. The little town at the inception of the company obligated itself very heavily to the extent of $100,000 odd for the purchase of a site on which to establish this organization. At the time of the inception of that company we were led to believe that it had an exceptionally bright future. It was situated at tidewater within easy access of coal deposits and iron ore and in a particularly good situation to manufacture iron and steel cheaply. As a result of that the stock of the company was very largely marketed. The Liberal governments of that day both of Nova Scotia and of the Dominion at Ottawa assisted the corporation very generously. The federal government afforded them a certain measure of tariff protection and also gave them bonuses which had the effect of stimulating industry in its early days.
The city of Sydney in order to meet the growing demand of the population also went heavily into debt to the extent of some millions of dollars in order to provide the necessary civic services for this great corporation. The population grew from 3,500 to

25,000. At the present time there are some 3,000 employees in that corporation, not all on full time, but all depending for their livelihood on it. There are several allied industries which depend upon it. For instance the Tar and Chemical Company, the Cross Fertilizer Company and some smaller industries depend for their existence upon the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, Limited. The Dominion Coal Company alone gets a market for about 1,250,000 tons of its coal there. In addition to those millions that the city has spent on services, trust and loan companies have spent other millions of dollars in mortgages and other securities in the city of Sydney. If this industry goes, all those industries go, all this money invested in stock, city bonds, stocks of other allied industries and mortgages in the city, go. So that when I contemplate the threatened failure of this industry as it is now threatened by the action of the directors who say that they can no longer carry on and pay the interest on their bonds, I shudder to think of the widespread disaster that must follow.
I think this government can save the situation and I am imploring them to do it. I am pointing out to them that this corporation is a child of Liberal administrations in the past. Its birth and growth were due to them and in years gone by they pointed with pride to the result of Liberal administration in Canada in the establishment, organization and carrying on of those great companies. To me the thing absolutely transcends all political interests. It is so important that I approach it entirely from a national standpoint. It is not my purpose to indicate how I think the government should act; that I leave entirely to them. It is not my purpose to insinuate even in the most indirect way that the situation is due to the action or inaction of any government in the past. I intend simply to point out the present situation, the disaster that threatens that company, and to ask the government if they will give us any assurance that this great disaster may be averted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What would my hon. friend recommend should be done?

As I pointed out I leave that entirely in the hands of the Prime Minister and his government. It would be presumptuous of me to indicate in any way what they should do. They are advised of the situation and they

Dominion Iron and Steel
probably know as much about it as I do. I feel sure' also that they are as much concerned about it as I am and that they will do whatever they deem fit. I leave it to their wisdom, because on their shoulders will rest the responsibility.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. W. JOHNSTONE (Cape Breton North-Victoria):
speechtext:
I rise to second the motion of the hon. member, and in doing so I heartily endorse every statement he has made. The only excuse, if excuse is necessary, for bringing up the matter is that it is one of vast importance to the Maritime provinces. I do not think the government and the members of this House generally realize quite fully what it means to those provinces to have either of our two basic industries closed down. It would throw out of employment some 3,000 men who are entirely dependent upon the operations of the industry, and, in addition to this, the market for local produce which supplies the needs of these miners would be affected. Small business firms, various minor industries, and citizens of all classes living in the surrounding districts are vitally interested in the coal and steel industries of Nova Scotia. The people of the province as well' as others in eastern Canada have also invested their money in the bonds, debentures and stocks of the company. I have personal knowledge of some who have sunk their savings in the industry, and the closing down of operations would mean ruin to them. Our steel works have passed through a very trying time during the past number of years. By reason of the situation on the seaboard the industry has suffered more than any other steel industry on this continent from the competition of European producers, which competition has been stimulated by depreciated currency abroad. This disability cannot last forever, but it may continue long enough to kill the industry in Nova Scotia. We therefore come to the government to-day and ask them to do something to solve this great problem. Definite action is needed right away to give the people of the province, and especially those engaged in these industries, some assurance of stability. I cannot do better than quote in this connection the words of an editorial which I have taken from one of the principal newspapers of Nova Scotia and which I think covers the ground completely:
The greatest industrial interests of the province are in jeopardy; an untoward result means for the worker poverty, for the owners of these properties ruin, and for the enterprising communities which have grown up around them desolation and decay. Such results are not local in their consequences. They affect the whole business life of the Dominion. May they do more, they affect the prestige of Canada.
We are asking the government to take hold of this matter in earnest, to investigate the facts, and to adopt such means as will render impossible such a condition as is predicted in this editorial. The situation in which the industry finds itself to-day is so serious that in a very short time unless relief is forthcoming the province of Nova Scotia will be injuriously affected, with the possibility of the city of Sydney being wiped off the map.
Mr. ROBERT K. SMITH (Cumberland): As a Nova Scotian I cannot sit idly by and allow this discussion to pass without offering some comment. The point raised by the hon. member who moved the resolution is well taken: this matter should be approached in a non-partisan spirit. The situation is so grave that, as he observes, it transcends all political affiliations and I have no doubt that we are capable of considering it from the national standpoint and from that standpoint alone.
The coal and steel industries of Nova Scotia have been very closely associated for the past number of years, so that what affects one industry naturally reacts upon the other. A blow to the steel industry of Nova Scotia is a blow to the coal industry of the same province, and vice versa. When we realize that these are the staple enterprises of that province, employing over 25,000 workmen, and that upon them over one-fifth of the entire population of the province is directly dependent, not to mention the other people in the province who are indirectly affected, we can understand how important it is to the province that nothing shall be done to impair their activity. I do not think there is any need just now to elaborate the circumstances which have hastened the present situation, but it can fairly be said that the steel industry of Nova Scotia, while it can compete with legitimate English or American industry, cannot meet the competition of European countries where cheapened labour, a depreciated currency and non-union conditions, and in a good many instances, child labour, make for a low cost of production.

What has the depreciated currency to do with foreign competition?
Mr. iSMITH: It has been stated by those who are in a position to know that the wages of the steel workers in Europe have increased to six times the value of the franc which is not on gold coin basis while in Canada the wages of steel workers have gone up 80 per cent on the basis of the gold standard. This
Dominion Iron and Steel

means that whereas the wages of European workers have increased six times on the basis of the franc, the increase is but 2 per cent on the basis of the gold coin. On the same standard the wages of the steel workers of Canada have increased to the enormous extent I have mentioned.

To the extent to which currency in foreign countries has depreciated, the cost of living has increased. Therefore the workman would have to secure a proportionately larger amount of money. I am not arguing on the general question that the hon. gentleman is discussing at'all, but I fail to see his point, that the European manufacturer is in a favoured position because of the depreciated currency of his country.

I think my friend will admit, taking that one point alone, that since 1913 we have increased the wages of our employees 80 per cent to meet the situation on a certain gold coin basis, which is the only basis we appear to be able to work on in Canada to-day, but with only a two per cent increase on the same gold basis in Belgium and France we are up against a disadvantage that we cannot very well overcome without some change.

Would the hon.
gentleman state what the importation of steel from Europe has been for the last year or two?

I have the information, but
I cannot put my hand on it at the moment. Our total importations of iron products for the year ending February, 1926, amount to $171,000,000 odd, of which we imported from the United States $151,000,000 odd, and from the United Kingdom $17,000,000 odd. I cannot give my hon. friend exact figures of the importations from European countries.

The depreciated
currency, then, does not enter very largely into the matter when you consider the imports.

It is a well-recognized fact,
and I think my hon. friend will admit it, that large steel importations have come from Belgium and France.

Not according to
the figures the hon. gentleman presented to the House.

What figures does my hon.
Mend refer to?
rMr, Smith.]
Of the total importations from the different countries, $171,000,000 odd, the gentleman stated that $151,000,000 odd came from the United States.

I hope my hon. friend is
not trying to take an advantage because I do not happen to have before me the figures of importations from the European countries. I have given the total importations.

It is merely a
matter of mathematics as to how much 'is left.

I do not think so. I did
not give my hon. friend complete figures.

W7ould the hon.
member say whether the importations in recent years have been more or less than they were before 1913?

Since 1913 the steel industry in Canada has suffered considerably; and whether the importations have been more or less I do not think is pertinent to the question that affects us to-day, because it is recognized that we are in a position which we cannot overcome under the existing circumstances.

It has a direct
bearing on the hon. gentleman's statement with regard to the effect of depreciated currency.

Does my hon. friend want
to convey the impression to the House that there are no importations from the European countries?
No; on the contrary, I am trying to get from the hon gentleman whether the importations have not been a great deal less.
Whether they have been less or not is not material if the situation is very seriously affected, as it is.

It is material to
the hon. member's argument.

I do not think so. I am
arguing that importations of iron products are coming from European countries with depreciated currency, and those importations are putting our manufacturers out of business. Now thlat situation may have existed in 1913, as my hon. friend says, more of the iron and steel products of European countries may have been imported then, but other elements may have entered into the matter then which would not affect it so adversely as to-day.

Dominion Iron and, Steel
Some figures have been handed me of importations from European countries. For the fiscal year ending March 31, 1924, the importations of steel billets from France and Belgium were 3,498 tons; for the same period in 1925, 5,628 tons; and for the ten months of 1925-26, 10,559 tons. These figures indicate a very marked increase.

Would the hon.
gentleman give the proportion of steel billets to the total steel imported?

I am not an expert on this
question and cannot supply the information requested.
The figures do not mean anything unless we have that information, Mr. Speaker.

The figures I have quoted
surely mean something. They show a very marked increase of importations in that particular line, and it is a line that seriously affects us in Nova Scotia. With respect to the importations of steel from Belgium, in my home town of Amherst, Nova 4 p.m. Scotia, we have been endeavouring for some time to carry on a rolling mill for the manufacture of reinforcing rods, using scrap steel in the process. Usually there is a ready market for this product. I wish to quote from a letter that I have received from one of the officials of the company to show what this industry is up against by way of foreign competition. He says:
I went down to Halifax on Tuesday and found the city full of Belgian bars. A certain company have received 725 tons, and all the jobbers of course are going there for supplies.
He mentions the name of the firm, but I do not wish to publish it. He states further: Apparently the company, and possibly a number of other concerns, have bought Belgian bars, and as far as I know we have never been asked to name a price. However, it is impossible ifor us to compete with the continental product to-day, and if this kind of thing is allowed to continue, it simply means that as far as the Maritimes is concerned our rolling mill is out of business. In fact it is a serious condition in Montreal as well.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I need stress the very serious and unsettled situation existing to-day in the Maritimes on account of the announcement of far-reaching con-[DOT] sequence which the big iron and steel company has been forced to make. Unless something is done by the government we will be very seriously affected in the province of Nova Scotia, and indirectly the whole Dominion will be adversely affected. Therefore I wish to appeal, as did the hon. gentlemen
who have preceded me, to the government to adopt whatever ways and means they deem to be most effective to avoid the very critical situation that is now impending in Nova Scotia.

May I ask the
hon. gentleman one question. He spoke of the unfair competition of Belgian workers. The steel workers of Nova Scotia have been working twelve hours a day. Would he suggest that the Belgian workers are working longer hours?

From the information I have they do not appear to have any regular hours of work over there. To a great extent it appears to be non-union labour and, as mentioned before, starvation-driven labour. That is the sort of competition we are up against to-day. I am not in a position to say what hours they work in Belgium, but I think it is a pretty safe guess that they work longer hours there than they do in Nova Scotia.
I fancy the hon. gentleman is chiefly guessing.
Could the hon. gentleman tell us whether or not it is true that Besco has discontinued buying Canadian-made nail kegs because they can buy to better advantage in the United States?
Why shouldn't they?
I cannot answer my hon. friend's question.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I have very much to add to the discussion. I did make some remarks outside the House, in the city of Toronto, in connection with the situation in Nova Scotia for which I was afterwards very strongly criticized in this House by one of the members from Nova Scotia. I made the statement at that time that something was wrong with the coal and steel industry in Nova Scotia, that apparently there was something economically wrong with the industry, that it was not on a sound basis. I wonder just what is the matter. We are having a discussion thi3 afternoon and we are told that something has got to be done to save the coal and steel industry in the province of Nova IScotia. But if <they are carrying on under proper conditions, if economically they are on a sound basis, just what is the trouble? Hon. gentlemen who have spoken want the government (to do something. That is pretty nebulous. I do not know what "something" means. I think
Dominion Iron and Steel

the members from Nova Scotia who are asking the government to do something should tell us what they want done.
In regard to what has been said about depreciated currency, that is a favourite argument in the House. I am willing to admit that there may be something in it, but not nearly as much, I think, as some hon. gentlemen would have us believe. If the workers in Great Britain work longer hours, work faster, and do not live as well, then probably they can compete at an advantage, but I question very much if they would under those circumstances. What does experience show? It shows that well-paid workers, living and working under proper conditions, can and do compete successfully with those who are not working under proper conditions. We are continually hearing one side of the argument, about depreciated currency and a low standard of living in Europe, and then hon. gentlemen immediately turn to the other side and speak of the high wages paid in the United States, and say that we cannot compete with the United States under the conditions they have there. Those two arguments do not harmonize.
I am forced to the conclusion that there is something wrong with the industries in the province of Nova Scotia, and I am quite willing to hear a statement of the conditions as they exist in that province. Let hon. gentlemen tell us plainly what is the matter with these industries. Not one hon. member has yet told us what is the matter with them. Let them tell us that plainly, and not get behind some other thing that perhaps i3 not the reason why these industries are. not able to compete. Nova Scotia is the oldest province of the Dominion, and it has done a lot for Canada. I sympathize with the people there.
Before the hon. gentleman proceeds, he says that there is something wrong with the industry. Will he not tell us what it is, and not be so nebulous?
Perhaps they are working under wrong economic conditions; perhaps they are over-capitalized.
Perhaps not.
Perhaps is not good enough.
I want hon. gentlemen from Nova Scotia to tell me what is the matter. They tell us that these industries cannot exist, and I do not know that I am called upon to make clear what the trouble is.
The hon. gentleman makes insinuations that are not fair. He ought to say what he means by those insinuations, and be frank and straightforward about it.

I do not know what I am insinuating. Hon. gentlemen from Nova Beotia tell us that these industries cannot exist, and I want them to tell us why they cannot exist. Some explanations have been given, but they do not sufficiently explain to me why the failure of the British Empire Steel Company is in the immediate offing. There is something more to explain. There must be some reason for this condition at the present time.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us whether he, as leader of his party, has seen the clear and distinct representations made by the Steel Company themselves as to what was wrong with that industry?

I do not know that I can
begin to answer questions in that way, but I think that people who really love their native province and understand some of the difficulties down there in Nova Scotia should explain to the House what the difficulty is. I do not think the House has ever been told. I do not think it is my province to tell the House exactly what is wrong with these industries. We have a large population depending upon these industries, and it will be very serious for them if they are thrown out of employment, and I am prepared to go a long way to help those people. I have sympathy for them. I might even be prepared to sacrifice some of my principles to help them. I do not wish to be held up here as antagonistic to the workers down in Nova Scotia. I simply would like to know what is the trouble. We know that these two industries are linked together, but no one has told the House whether the coal industry is leaning on the steel, or whether the steel industry is leaning on the coal. I have never had that made clear yet. We want to know something of the economic conditions under which these industries are being carried on, and I repeat, there is something economically wrong, because these industries have received tremendous bounties in the past, a vast amount of money that I cannot name, and yet we find ourselves in the position to-day of being called upon to do something to rescue the industry from approaching bankruptcy; in fact, they are bankrupt. Would a little assistance really remedy the situation? Would the company not in a year or two find itself again in its present condition? Let us get

Dominion Iron and Steel
down to the basic facts and find out what is wrong. I repeat again, I am not antagonistic to these industries nor to the people dependent upon them. I am very friendly to the people of Nova Scotia, but I would like to know what are the basic facts underlying their difficulties. Can we possibly remedy them by paltry assistance in the meantime to get over a difficult situation? I hope some member from Nova Scotia will get down to basic facts, and tell us what is really the matter with the coal and steel industry in his province.

We are
face to face with a situation that might have been expected by anyone who had in any way learned even the ABC of economics many years ago. It is a case where an industry built up on a false basis has come practically to the point where it has got to reorganize and be built upon a sure foundation, on its own merits and standing, or it can go no further. The steel industry in Canada has from its inception been favoured as perhaps no other industry has; in fact, I do not think that in any country in the world has the steel industry been favoured as it has in Canada, and I am not excepting the United States. I remember that when the Dominion Iron and Steel Company was first inaugurated it secured from this government pretty nearly everything that we could give it. In the first place, we gave it a protection of some 17i per cent on steel rails. Then the government of the province, or the municipalities, gave it thirty years' exemption from taxation. It got $7 a ton bounty on steel rails, and also got favoured railway rates throughout the Dominion, and any royalties supposed to have been collected on coal were repaid to the company. At that time there was a great steel trade going on in Canada owing to the tremendous amount of railway construction work in progress. The two great companies in Canada were then furnishing steel rails for the government sections of the Transcontinental railway. The government paid as high as $32 per ton for these rails. They also paid a bounty on production making altogether $39 a ton for the steel rails used on the government sections of the Transcontinental. At that very time one of these companies was cutting prices against the whole world, and delivering rails in India at a price of $24 a ton. Did they need protection to carry on in this country, or did they use the protective privileges we were giving them to enable them to deliver rails at $24 a ton in that distant land? Either the companies cannot compete abroad or they do not need pro-14011-282
tection at home. The charge has been levelled at us in this corner of the House during the last five years that we would destroy every industry in the country. We have no such intention, in fact I would not be averse to a little protection if it were simply the home market they needed.
Hear, hear.
Well done.

That statement pleases hon.
gentlemen.
Hear, hear.
The lost sheep.

But this is what I have to
say: If they needed protection to get the home market only nobody would have much objection to it, but the government for many years sought to give them a blanket protection to fleece the rest of the community. That being the case I say it is time to quit. When that stage is reached it becomes class privilege, and the granting of any privilege of this kind to one industry is done at the expense of other industries. I say that we have come to the point in this country where no industry must be privileged to tax other industries in order to keep itself going. If there is an industry in Canada which is essential to the national welfare it ought to be maintained but it should establish in the first place that its maintenance is a necessity to the country at large and that it needs protection. The 'hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald) admits that the British Empire Steel Corporation enjoys all the advantages of coal, ore, and of convenient transportation facilities; in fact if you look at the map of the world to-day you would think the industry was most advantageously situated for delivering its products to the markets of the world.
What then is wrong at the present time? Another hon. gentleman says the government can prevent a catastrophe from occurring but does not say how the government can do it. Can this industry ever stand on its own feet? After the lapse of thirty years it has shown that under present methods of manufacturing it cannot do so. We should consider now what is wrong. If hon. members in favour of protection cannot answer this question why do they not support a reference of the case to the Tariff Advisory Board in order to get at the root of the matter? It has been shown how important all the subsidiary industries are to this particular industry. Well, practically all industries in this country are sub-

Dominion Iron and Steel

sidiary to agriculture, because the latter is a basic industry. Actually agriculture is being destroyed to-day because of having to carry the other industries on its back. It has had to pay artificial prices, enhanced prices, for everything it has needed whereas for the things it produces it is compelled to face the competition of the world. The steel industry says it cannot compete with the cheap labour and the depreciated currencies of Europe. But we farmers with our own products have to compete against the cheap labour of the whole world, even the labour of Europe, Asia, India and the Argentine. In no other country in the world are such high prices being paid for articles needed on the farm as in Canada. When an hon. gentleman urges the importance of this matter on the House, and expresses a fear that the country does not appreciate its urgency, does he not see the importance of having every industiy stand on its own feet, and should he not refrain from insisting upon protection which will be ruinous to other industries? Industries should pay their way, but according to the tales of woe we have heard in this House for the last four or five months no industry engaged in manufacturing is able to stand on its own feet. What is wrong? Let us ask this question and try to answer it. The fact is that because of our fiscal policy, which has been a false one from the beginning, we keep the cost of production at too high a figure for successful competition in the markets of the world. To-day the industry of agriculture is being carried on at a loss. Somebody may ask how it has been possible for it to remain in this condition for so long a period. Agriculture has been mining the soil in this country for the last thirty years. The farmers have been mining the soil in order to satisfy the demand of the rest of the country and have been obliged to pay enhanced prices for everything they needed under the protective tariff.

If agriculture is carried
on at a loss why did the hon. member vote for a Speech from the Throne which stated it was very prosperous?
The right hon. gentleman is evading the issue. He knows very well that what I am stating is the case.
Does the hon. member say that the Speech from the Throne does not declare that agriculture is prosperous?

I was not speaking of the Speech from the Throne and do not intend to allude to it. The right hon. gentleman
I Mr. Evans.]
knows as well as any man in this House that even the agricultural industry cannot be carried on under present conditions. Because we had a good crop last year and conditions are a little better in the country, it is not to be inferred that agriculture is on a permanent basis of prosperity. Our manufacturing industries have had prosperous years in the past but they did not seek to put themselves on a sound footing; they relied on the price-fixing pow'er given them by the tariff to fleece the consumers. Then when they have destroyed their own market and lessened the purchasing power of those who are engaged in the primary industries they raise the cry that they are face to face with a catastrophe. Another hon. gentleman has declared that depreciated currency has killed the iron and steel industry. I ask this question : Does not the agricultural indutsry have to face depreciated currency as well as other industries?
The same hon. gentleman argues that the industry has been hurt by low wages. At the same time we are told that the country which pays the highest wages in the world and has no depreciated currency is one of our chief competitors, and there is a general unanimity of statement that we cannot compete with the United States in the matter of industrial production. If depreciated currency is a detriment and prevents us from competing in the markets of the world, surely a country where the currency is not deflated can be more easily competed with, but such is not the case. I think the iron and steel company have come to a point where they might consider retrenching. Either the output is too great or something is wrong with the fiscal policy if they are unable to pay wages and employ labour. The threat is so often made in this House that unless protection is maintained or increased capital will seek investment in other parts of the country, and our workmen will go to the United States. The fact of the matter is that they will not do anything of the kind, and a great many threats have been made even this year regarding the steel and automobile industries. In fact some of them shut down for a little while for no object except to create public opinion.
What is this catastrophe which is facing us now? is it anything more than to create public opinion, to obtain more protection and to gouge more money out of the pockets of the people? I do not know, but one thing is certain. The tariff in this country has destroyed the enterprise of our manufacturers, and to-day they are carrying on

Dominion Iron and Steel
with obsolete methods, and they prefer to follow any means whatsoever to create the impression that protection is needted and must be provided before they will look to their own house, change their methods and find their own market. It is a serious thing. Hon. members in this House point to the dole system in England, declaring that the workmen in England do not want to work as long as they get a dole. The whole of the manufacturing industry of Canada has depended on the dole for the last thirty-five years and now if it destroys the desire to work on the part of the British workman on the one hand it must on the other destroy enterprise on the part of employers and manufacturers.
I took a little trip down into Quebec the other day and I saw a product being mined and shipped to Eochester. I refer to feldspar. We have all that feldspar in that district, easily mined, with the power in the river close by, the cheapest power that can be got any place in the world, yet not one industry using that product in this country is established, and it finds its market in Rochester. I came down to Buckingham Junction Saturday night and found thirteen cars all loaded for a foreign market. We have no enterprise in this country. What is wrong with it? Why will people rely on the tariff and not on their own enterprise? Why will they continually pursue a false fiscal policy which puts the cost of doing everything entirely out of line with world prices and then come back and seek more protection?

My
only excuse for asking the House to bear with me now is the gravity of the situation referred to by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald) who introduced the motion. I have no intention of referring in any way at this time to the fiscal policy either of this government or of any past government in relation to the condition of affairs that now exists in Nova Scotia, though greatly tempted, in view of the remarks of some speakers to my left, to deal with that matter. I prefer however not to do so because I really do not want to make this a controversial question at this time. The gravity of the situation in Nova Scotia is certainly great. I may attribute it to one source and other hon. members may attribute it to another source. I am not going into that at this time. The fact is that the affairs of the British Empire Steel Corporation to-day are in a critical condition. Practically one-half the 14011-282^
population of Nova Scotia is in doubt and almost despair as to what the outcome is to be.
There is I think an idea in the House that the iron and steel industry of this country dates back to the inauguration of the Dominion Steel Corporation about the beginning of the present century, but I would like to point out that it goes back very considerably further. Open hearth steel was first made in this country at New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, in 1882 and the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company continued to produce steel in yearly increasing quantities until the absorption of that company in 1921 by the British Empire Steel Corporation. In the year 1900 the Scotia company acquired the property of the General Mining Association of London, England, who began operations at Sydney Mines, Cape Breton and at Albion Mines near New Glasgow, Pictou county in 1826 just a hundred years ago. In passing I may say coal has been exported from Nova Scotia for 254 years; at first in small quantities. Some thing has been said as regards the inter-dependency of the coal and the steel. I can tell the House that so far as the Dominion Steel Corporation is concerned, that corporation was founded entirely with the object of providing a home market for the slack coal which was then produced in quantities much beyond what it was then possible to find any market for on this continent. It is an entirely mistaken idea to suppose, as many do suppose, some inside this House and a very great many outside the House, that the steel corporation was and is being operated at the expense of the coal property. There is a figure which the steel companies ought to pay the coal companies for all the slack coal used quite irrespective of whether they are independent or inter-locking companies. But my point is that if you close down the steel plants in Nova Scotia there will soon accumulate a large quantity of slack or small coal for which no market is available.
Consider the position in Cape Breton prior to the establishment of the iron and steel industry. The situation was this: not over 15 or at the most 25 per cent of the slack coal produced could find a market. A large quantity was stowed in the goof under ground; dumps containing hundreds of thousands of tons were to be seen in close proximity to the coal mines, not only in Cape Breton but in Pictou and Cumberland counties-hundreds of thousands of tons in all for which there was then no market. I myself have bought slack coal in thousands of tons, tens of thousands of tons in the late eighties and nineties at ten and twelve cents

Dominion Iron and Steel
a ton. The price later went up to twenty-five cents, to fifty cents; it has gone up a great deal since that time; but the fact is that the coal industry of Nova Scotia cannot be carried on to-day without a steel industry supporting it. They are inter-dependent.
That is part of the information we have been seeking.

I am trying to give it
to the House.

there is such a large quantity of slack coal mean that there is more slack coal in the Nova Scotia mines than in other mines throughout the world?

It does not necessarily
mean anything of the kind. The quantity of slack coal produced in any particular field depends on the character of the coal and the method of mining.

Scotia coal is not of equal value to other coal?
It does not mean anything of the kind.

Then I cannot understand
the point.

There are I fear many
things the hon. gentleman cannot understand. I am sorry I cannot enlighten him in reference to everything.

Since the hon. gentleman
has made that remark, might I ask how it is that when representations are made to us to aid certain industries, it is definitely stated that Nova Scotia coal is not of equal value to other coal?
That statement is made by people who. have very little knowledge of the facts.
That statement is made by people who say they know.

It does not make any
difference whether they say they know or not if they really do not. An hon. member recently made certain assertions regarding the character of Nova Scotia coal. I say that they are not true. When you mine 5,000,000 tons of coal you must of necessity have a considerable quantity of slack, I do not care in what country or under what conditions the coal is mined. There is a difference between the quantity of slack produced in certain fields and from certain kinds of coal, but all coal mined produces a considerable
[Mr. Cantley.l
quantity of slack, some of which is used and some wasted unless there be nearby some coke consuming enterprise.
As regards the Belgium situation I am not going to deal at length with the question of depreciated currency, although it has a very important bearing on the facts notwithstanding what representations may be made in this House. The hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans), when he referred to the effect of depreciated currency in regard to farming, put his finger exactly on one of the factors bearing on the case. The franc to-day is worth less than four cents or about one-fifth of the nominal value. Labour is getting more in francs than it did before the war; but food in proportion to the gold value of the franc is very much lower in price than it was prior to the war, with the result that owing to the depreciation of the franc in their country Belgic work people are able to live more cheaply than they were before the war. We are not handicapped by the whole difference in the value of the franc, but we are to a considerable extent. Let us get down to concrete facts. Two steamer loads of Beligum wire rods have been landed in Cape Breton within the past year. Why? Because they could be and were landed there at a figure representing nine dollars a ton less than the cost of producing them in Sydney. Thousands of tons of Belgian billets, some French billets and some German billets and a large tonnage of skelp bars for pipe have been landed at Montreal for further manufacture. Why? Because the steel can be landed there under present conditions of labour, exchange and freight for less than we can produce them in Canada. I am not going to say who is to blame. I state only what are patent facts that cannot be disputed. That is one of the causes of the present difficulty.	-
One hon. gentleman says that agriculture is the most important industry in Canada. Undoubtedly it is; it is so in most countries. But next to agriculture the most vital industry in any country is the iron and steel industry. Reference has been made to the tax which the iron and steel industry imposes on agriculture. In view of the fact that the steel used in the manufacture of practically all implements used in agriculture is admitted into Canada free, what burden is the steel and iron industry on agriculture in this country?
I would like to make some little reference to the importance of the iron and steel industry in Canada looking back over the history of the last ten years. What happened

Dominion Iron and Steel
immediately after war was declared? We were asked whether we could supply certain munitions of war. How did we meet the demands upon us and what was the effect of our so meeting them? We were able to demonstrate that we could make in Canada basic steel which would meet all the requirements of the British War Office, though of a class of steel which they claimed and indeed was different from what they had' always used and which they were getting elsewhere; in short, they wanted acid steel of which none was made in Canada. They had certain specifications, certain tests. We met those specifications and tests both chemically and physically and we did it with basic steel, with the result that we were able in this country to embark on the production of munitions.
It is in the mind of all the leaders on both sides as to what that meant for Canada. It meant that hundreds of thousands of people were employed over a period of years. It doubled and quardrupled our exports within <1 eighteen months. It enabled us to earn money with which to prosecute the war. It gave employment to thousands of women and girls also to men who were incapacitated for service and who otherwise would have been idle. Not only did it create a great demand for iron steel and coal, but it extended its ramifications to almost every industry in this country, notably to the lumber industry, millions upon millions of feet of lumber being used in the production of boxes and cases for the export packing of munitions of various kinds. The outcome of the whole situation was that Canada was put in an industrial and exporting position that it never before occupied. The war profits taxes that came afterwards contributed very largely to meeting the expenses of the war. The steel and iron industry is fundamental, and essential to the national existence.
What is the situation in the United States? They are to-day making more than two-thirds of all the steel made in the world. Year after year for the past half dozen years on the average we have brought into this country nearly
700,000	tons of steel, or enough to provide work for every blas't furnace, every open hearth furnace and every steel mill in Canada. I do not want to get into the discussion of a national policy or any other policy; I want to get back to the fact confronting the industry to-day. The towns of New Glasgow and Trenton are dependent entirely upon that industry. One has a population of say 12,000 and the other has a population of about 8,000; they both have all modem conveniences, tramways, paved streets and so on.
In the town of Sydney Mines, which has a population of about 12,000, not a wheel has turned, not a furnace has been lighted since 1921 when the Nova Scotia Steel Company came under the control of the British Empire Steel Corporation. I know there will be a difference of opinion as to what is to blame for the present situation, whether it as due to management or tariff. I am not going to discuss that now. What I want to discuss is this. We are up against not a matter of opinion, but concrete facts. Tens of thousands of people in the eastern part of Nova Scotia to-day are in doubt whether they are to continue to get a living where they now live and have their homes. Hundreds are absolutely ruined. The government has a duty in the present situation. I am asking them to take at once what steps they can to give some measure of relief to a section of the country which is looking to them for help. Some bon. gentlemen may say it is incumbent upon me to suggest to the government what they should do in the circumstances. I am advised that proposals have been submitted to the government as to what they are or how far they go I am not fully informed and if I were so informed I would prefer not to discuss them here; indeed I fancy the government would perhaps not care to have them discussed. What I here and now ask is that the government take adequate, effective and immediate action to meet the critical condition which now faces one-half of the population of my native province,

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
There were some other speakers who desired to express their views. However, I wish to make a few observations on the situation as it stands. It was quite evident from the address of the hon. gentleman who introduced the subject (Mr. MacDonald) that he was most anxious to avoid any post mortem into the causes, various though they may be, which have led to the present unfortunate pass in relation to the steel industry in the province of Nova Scotia. Very carefully he assigned no responsibility, and he did so not because he did not feel that responsibility rested with well-known parties and well-known governments, but because he was desirous of finding a
remedy for the present and not of censuring in respect to the past.
I do not think the seriousness of the position could be better stated than in the terms of the hon. member himself. When a city of
25,000	people, as well as other towns of less dimensions, depend wholly for their existence upon this industry and upon this company, and when, as well, communities further distant are dependent upon allied industries, it becomes only too evident that if Nova Scotia is to have a chance at all in the years that are before us, we cannot sit silently by and disinterestedly allow this industry to fall. Sometimes commercial collapses are of such dimensions that whatever may have been the original causes, however various may have been the foundation causes of the malady, it becomes a national question whether or not we should stand by and allow a crash. The late government found itself in that position in relation to more than one enterprise; in relation to the Canadian Northern enterprise in the first place. We could have stood by and permitted the collapse of that great business entity. Had we done so and the result been merely local or individual we could have been justified. Had we been able to do so and left the nation as a whole better off than by any other course we might have taken, it would have been our duty to stand aside and let matters take their course. The same situation presented itself in relation to the Grand Trunk Pacific, end again in relation to the Grand Trunk. In much less forceful degree but nevertheless with considerable menace, it presented itself also in relation to the Quebec and Saguenay railway along the north shore of the St Lawrence. In each of these cases we felt that we were not in any way responsible for the situation as it had developed. We might very well have washed our hands of the whole affair and said others were responsible for the agreements that had generated the enterprises, and that therefore we had nothing to do with the consequences. But we felt it was not well to take that rather complacent, attitude, and we addressed ourselves to trying to solve the problem that presented itself, and to seeing that the least possible disaster ensued to the people of Canada. The present situation seems to be of much the same kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The industries my right hon. friend referred to were railways.

Yes, those which I have mentioned.
Dominion Iron and Steel

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With respect to which there is more or less of a federal obligation-I mean primarily?

In the case of the Quebec and Saguenay railway I do not think there was any federal obligation. At all events it was not the fact of a federal obligation that influenced our action; it was the immensity and far-reaching character of the disaster that would ensue; it was the extent of the repercussion which would permeate almost every branch of Canadian activity. We asked ourselves would there be greater injury caused by this than would result from the imposition of the burden which we called upon the country to sustain. Here the situation relates to an industry which appears to be localized to the province of Nova Scotia. It is not wholly so localized; Canadians everywhere are interested in the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, in the foundations of that industry in the eastern province. But even if it were localized to Nova Scotia it is of so immense a character and its results are going to be so crucial that it behooves this House to examine the situation and see if there is anything we can do. I do not want to traverse the inquiry which is again insisted upon by the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) as to what the causes are of the present situation. I will make a few references to what has been said in that regard but they will be very brief.
I do not think the causes can be named in any single sentence. The causes are more than one, I would say, fundamentally though they allot themselves into two catalogues: first, tariff; second, transportation. But I do not seek to give the House the impression that in these two fields alone are to be found the whole of the original reasons for the present position. I do not know but what, perhaps, some may be looked for in the field of management. At the same time I am of the view that you might concede a very great deal in the way of better management and still you would has this position at the present time, or very little later, on account of the other two causes themselves. Hon. members of course have argued, particularly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that the condition cannot be attributed to anything in the way of government policy, because he is able to look at one steel company in Canada and say that that company has succeeded. Well, if this is to be taken as an answer and as a vindication of government policy, then government policy never can be wrong. I do not care what government policy you have
TMr. Meighen.]
in this Dominion in relation to any commercial matter whatever. I do not care what fiscal policy you have, you cannot have any fiscal policy under which there will not be some company in some industry succeed. With the advantages this country possesses, with the type of its citizenship, with the enterprise we have, there will always be some company which will succeed under any conditions. But he who is satisfied with the condition of the steel industry as an industry in Canada to-day, especially when he compares it with the progress made by our great competitor, is either a very small Canadian or else he is so blinded by politics that he is satisfied with anything under his own party.
The steel industry of Canada to-day is struggling and almost staggering. I know the Steel Company of Canada has had a measure of prosperity. I do not know that I can very fully, as a business man could, assign the special reasons which apply to that company, but I know that it is engaged in successful production, which production has a limited market in this Dominion; others cannot engage in it for the reason that the market is not here-classes of production which in a considerable degree are protected by the tariff even as it stands now, lines of production that are not comparable in very many important respects with those that are followed by the Algoma Steel Company and the great industry of Nova Scotia, the other two elements of steel production in our country. The minister was happily ignorant of the condition of affairs in the Algoma company. He is never prepared with any statistics that cast the least reflection upon the specially well selected figures he produces himself. He does not know anything about them, and he led the House to believe that if the British Empire Steel Corporation had had a management which would have produced'the Cover-dale report, or if it had less capitalization, nil would have been well with them. The fact of the matter is that this Dominion of Canada now, in the great articles of steel production, is only producing 68 per cent-that was the figure in the very latest report I was able to get-of what it produced I think in the year 1913, at all events in the year which has already been mentioned in Hansard in the speech of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett). That is the production of the steel industry of our country, a production which compares only as two-thirds of what we produced years ago. The United States, our great competitor, in the same time are producing 60 per cent more than they produced previously.

Dominion Iron and Steel

largely.
Those were long before, and they would not amount to one-tenth of one per cent. That is about the size of the mind of the hon. member for Pontiac.

They would not amount to that. In 1921 our production was 64 per cent of what it was in 1913. The United States production the same year was exactly 64 per cent, showing that they shared in that world depression with ourselves, but they sprung out of it immediately, and from that day to this their production has gone steadily ahead until to-day they are 60 odd per cent over what they were before, while we are just 68 per cent of what we were before. We are still struggling-
Will my right hon. friend not admit that in 1913 we were over-producing a great deal?

I would not admit it, I do not think it is true. I cannot say I have given special study to that matter. We were importing at that time, and we had a hint from the hon. member for Weyburn that we were importing more then than now, but I think he is wrong. It seems to me we were not producing enough then, and are not now either. Those are the general conditions. Under our tariff to-day 15 per cent of all that is produced by the three great steel companies of our country, the British Empire, the
Dominion Iron and Steel

Steel Company of Canada and the Algoma Steel Company, is either imported free or given the benefit of a 99 per cent rebate on the importation. Under this situation we find our largest company shivering right on the brink of the precipice while the great companies of the United States are enjoying a prosperity never before known in their history. Whatever the causes may be, hon. members cannot complacently sit down and say: Oh, that is because we have not good enough men here, or because there is too much capital in this company.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend is not insinuating that I said the men were not good enough.
No, but my hon. friend did intimate that the management was not good enough, and management usually consists of men.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I challenge my right hon.
friend to find where I said anything of the kind.
I accept my hon. friend's explanation, but I ask him to chide the rest of his followers when they give that as the cause, because that is all the 'cause I have heard given this afternoon.
I think the right hon. member himself admitted that something might be due to management.

It may be, but that is not the fundamental cause. The great fundamental causes are different, and they are to be found in the field of tariff and transportation. The hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) asked: What is the matter with the Canadian people? Or rather he would not put it so widely as that because he never included the farmers of the west in his query. He asked: "What is the matter with the Canadian manufacturers? They have no enterprise. I saw thirteen cars of feldspar somewhere in the province of Quebec going down to the United States to be manufactured." I ask the hon. member for Rosetown, as well as other hon. members: Does he think there has been some special virus or poison or disease that has affected one selected portion of our population and rendered them inferior to their competitors, while the rest of us are all right?
Yes.

He does. I do not think that does credit to the hon. member's intelligence, so whenever he asks me I will relieve him of the sentence he uttered this afternoon. Our manufacturing population is recruited

chiefly from our agriculturists. If the hon. member looks to-day at those men upon whose shoulders rests the burden of our great manufacturing enterprises, within whose brains develop those great enterprises, he will find them the sons of agriculturists. He will find right in the offices, right on the directorates of the greatest manufacturing industries of our country, men who were very recently farmers or the sons of farmers.
I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman if they have not brains to stand on their own feet now.

If they had not brains they would not be where they are, so the reason cannot be lack of brains. Some of them are not where they are, if I may use the Irish expression. They are over there and when you find them over there, they are right at the top. Indeed many sons of Canadian farmers are to-day at the top of great enterprises in the United States. If you put the Canadian enterprise on a footing where it has a chance to compete with the United States enterprise, they will be here and not in the United States. You 'may preach enterprise all you like; you cannot found an enterprise and force it ahead if the fundamental conditions surrounding your competitor are better than those surrounding yourself.
The right hon. member has struck the nail on the head right there.
I certainly have, and I hope the hon. member for Brandon will strike the same nail on the same head. That is exactly the head he has been missing for many a year.

Will the hon. member let me put myself right? He referred to the fundamentals in connection with industry. If the coal is as good and the materials are as good and there is some protection, what is the matter?
It is all a matter of what is "some," but I congratulate the hon. member for Brandon on his progress. I have no difficulty in remembering the time when he would not even countenance some protection.
I do not think so.

I remember when he
would never sound the word except by way of anathema, when he used to make the welkin of the school houses ring against protection in any form. Think of the progress the hon. member for Rosetowm has made! We would

Dominion Iron and Steel
not hear it suggested that protection was necessary for the home market. My heart took a leap of joy when I heard from the hon. member for Rosetown. When I get him that distance there is not much left in the way of conversion of the entire House of Commons.
I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman again: What are the fundamentals of industry?

I would say:	Common
sense, conditions comparable with those of one's competitors, and hard work. The hon. member has the hard work. I will not deny him common sense. Just come along with the third requisite.

Is that all the right hon.
gentleman is asking for to put industry on a safe basis just now, or is he asking for more tariff protection?

Why are they not in this
country?

'I have been trying to
explain to the hon. member that it is because we have had a population filled by false doctrine who have turned policy in the wrong
direction, or, where not turned in the wrong direction, have failed to follow courageously through a true policy.

How long is it since we
have been under a protectionist policy in this country?

It is only five years
since hon. gentlemen opposite came into power, but it seems fifty to the country.

It seems so to my right
hon. friend because he is out of office, but not to anyone else.

It was the country I
was feeling for, not myself.
I think the right hon. member comes first in his feelings,

I want to make a reference to a statement which came from the Minister of Finance, who said that this House has decided that higher and higher and still higher protection was not to be the policy of Canada. For myself, although I have listened carefully to the voices of Canadian parties and people, I have never heard anyone suggest that that should be the policy of Canada. I have heard it suggested that a definite, sound policy of protection applicable to all Canadian production should be our policy; that it should be frankly carried through; that it should be pursued rigorously and thoroughly; that it should be adhered to definitely and consistently year after year, and that all these thunderings and lightnings against it should cease, so that confidence among our business men might be restored. I have never heard anyone talk about higher and higher and still higher protection save those who, afraid of a true statement of the Conservative doctrine, always seek to misrepresent it in order to have something to attack. It does not follow that, even after repeated reductions in many important lines, merely because we want protection restored in those lines we therefore want a high tariff, because if a high tariff follows from a raising of the tariff in any particular, then it must follow that free trade must be the logical policy of those who are preaching freer trade. If those who want higher protection on certain lines of Canadian products are to be denominated high protectionists by hon. gentlemen opposite, then those who preach freer trade must be denominated free traders. The Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Mackenzie King) has preached "freer trade ' in that very language, and he has preached it frequently in this Dominion. But if I were to call him free trader there is no language
Dominion Iron and Steel

which would be vicious enough for him to apply to me. 1 ask to be treated in the same way as we treat hon, gentlemen opposite. They are in favour of a continuous lowering of the tariff; we are in favour of no such thing. We are in favour of necessary protection for Canadian industry, whatever that protection may be. But because we are in favour of that measure of protection we do not want to be called higher and higher and still higher protectionists every hour of the day.

The right hon. gentleman
says that the Conservative party stands for adequate protection, but I have yet to hear any hon. member say what adequate protection actually is. Does it mean such protection as will absolutely prevent foreign products from coming into Canada?
Nothing of the sort. It is protection at a level which shall put the Canadian industry on a parity with its competitor.
Brick for brick.

That does not follow at all. The United States might have a high duty on something on which we did1 not need a duty at all, and they might have no tariff whatever on something upon which it would be necessary for us to impose a duty. They have to-day no tariff whatever on some things on which we must necessarily have a tariff if we are to have any Canadian production.
I cannot recall who it was, but I rather think it was the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) who sought to give the House the impression that we had not so good a quality of coal in Nova Scotia, and that this probably accounted for the trouble. If I were asked any question in regard to the respective qualities of Canadian and American coal I could not answer it, but the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) has said that while there is a large proportion of what is called slack coal in the Canadian mines, such coal is to be found in mines elsewhere. It is of course obvious that some mines are better than others, and I should be obliged ;o concede that great areas of American coal are better in quality than the Canadian product. But I do want this to sink into the mind of the hon. member for Lisgar, as well as others, that even if that is true it is not good business, it is not common sense on the part of this country to buy the better article from another country if we can use the inferior product ourselves.
I was trying to find out if it was true, that is all.

I do not think the hon. member went further than that, but still I believe the lesson is necessary even though he did not give immediate evidence of its need. I ask hon. gentlemen this question: Even though we have not quite as good coal as is to be found in the great anthracite fields of the United States, is it not better economics, is it not more thrifty, is it not wiser for Canada so to direct its policy as to consume its own coal rather than buy the superior article from a foreign land? Let me illustrate. Suppose the hon. member had a farm and on that farm he had a supply of coal which was not as good as Pennsylvania anthracite but which nevertheless was of fair quality and quite fit for use. Would it be thrifty of him and his family to purchase American coal of high quality and ignore his own because he was not enterprising enough to dig it from the ground and use it for the purposes of his farm? The illustration is a simple and homely one, but it applies to countries as much as to families. And unless we have common sense and business acumen enough so to direct our policy that our own coal fields will be exploited, thus saving scores of millions of dollars which heretofore have gone to other lands, we shall continue in that difficult situation portrayed by the hon. member for South Cape Breton and other gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon.
All through these years, in 1922, 1923, 1924 and 1925, we have been gradually lowering the tariff, and now we find ourselves face to face with a crash in what is perhaps the greatest single enterprise in Canada outside the railways. What is the remedy? I am not going to say that an immediate remedy can be found wholly along one line. Sometimes you get to a pass where you are bound to explore other possibilities than the one which seems obvious. I know certain appeals have been made by the industry-appeals recited, perhaps not quite completely, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) this afternoon. I know, too, that objection can be offered to many, if not all, of them. But sometimes we have to overcome such objections, and by whatever means we have at our disposal we must avoid a great calamity, knowing that though the objections be considerable it is far wiser to surmount them than to encounter disaster itself. I promise the government that any suggestions they may put forward we shall approach in a sympathetic mood. We want this industry saved. I implore the government to exert its best ability, in the light of the best inform-

Dominion Iron and Steel
ation it has, to meet the situation. I assure them that though we cannot promise to endorse their proposals, if they are the worst we shall at least review them in a sympathetic frame of mind; and certainly it is our earnest hope that we shall find ourselves able to support them.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Hon. members will .recall
that timie and again this industry has come to the attention of the country. Only last year its workers came here asking for a small amount to tide them over their period of unemployment, and we were told then that this was entirely a provincial matter. Now Besco itself waits upon the government with a request for a handout of $500,000 or $300,000. There have been many investigations into the coal .and steel industry of Nova Scotia, at least in certain aspects, but we have never yet had an investigation into the finances of the company, and until the financial affairs of this concern are disclosed to the country the government in my opinion is quite right in refusing any assistance. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) takes the view that the company must trust the members of the government. He should go further, and declare that before one red cent more is given to Besco the financial situation of the company shall be made public.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has referred to the tariff and transportation. I submit there are other matters to which reference should be made and which have been lightly touched upon to-day. Again and again we have had the most extraordinary representations from Besco. Those who spoke for the company last year assured us then that within a few weeks everything would be lovely. Mr. Kyte, later followed by Mr. Carroll, had something to say with regard to the situation. On February 24, 1925, as reported in Hansard at page 488, Mr. Kyte said:
The question of unemployment, therefore, is about settled so far as Sydney and Glace Bay are concerned.
If this despatch is true, and I believe it ds; if the steel plant will soon be working on a basis of 100 per cent production, then there will be employment for every steel worker in ithe city of Sydney, and for every coal (miner in the county of Cope Breton. That is the happiest solution of our difficulty, and I think the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg might very well allow the matter to drop with (the assurance given in this despatch that unemployment will cease entirely and that the plant will be working (full time by the sixteenth of March.
These are the representations we have had from time to time. We have had only a mere reference to-day to the over-capitaliza-14011-283
tion of this company. Anyone might have gone further and said that the whole company has been a splendid example of frenzied finance. We have had very little said of the mismanagement that has characterized the operations of this corporation. Charges have been made before on the floor of the House in other connections in regard to this matter. The very fact that we have had such industrial trouble in the steel and .coal industry during the last few years is of itself indicative that the men .in charge of this big corporation are not fitted for such responsibility. I have spoken again and again in this House on behalf of the steel and coal workers of Nova Scotia.
I may say that it has been more than a surprise to me to receive letters from the shareholders of this concern thanking me for having done something to expose the situation that prevails in Nova Scotia, because they realize that if the existing conditions continue they are sure to lose their investment in the company, that even the bondholders will lose their capital.
I need not go into the exploitation which the company has practised against the workers. It is only a few days ago that in this House we had to protest against more coal miners being imported from the Old Country. Surely those in control of the company must know its affairs, and yet they were proposing to bring in many more miners because they say the mining industry is growing at such a rate that they must have a larger number of miners to carry on the work, and then in regard to the steel workers, again and again we have stated in this House that they have been worked eleven and thirteen hours shifts, and every other wedk twenty-four hours on end. Yet we were told to-day by one hon. gentleman who was speaking on behalf of the company that this industry could not stand competition with the product of the low-paid: workers of Europe. I think the hon. Minister of Finance has answered the main part of that contention, that there is comparatively little importation of steel products from Belgium. There is the other side of the question. Statements were made that in Belgium men were working very long hours, that there was child labour and that very low standards of living prevailed. I would point out that since June 1921 Belgium has had a very stringent eight-hour day in force.
Mr, CANTLEY: Does the hon. gentleman wish the House to understand that the workers in Belgium during the last three or four years, or since the war, have been confined to an eight-hour day?

Dominion Iron and Steel
Yes. I should like to read a protest-

Will' he let me make a
statement?
Order.

I am making the
statement just now. I have only a minute or two more at my disposal. I hold in my hand one of the publications of the International Labour office of the League of Nations, to which we are a contributing member. This is dated May 31, 1926, and the hon. gentleman will find in it a strong protest on behalf of some of the employers of Belgium to the effect that they are in a very awkward position in regard to the eight-hour day because they are forced to compete with nations whose labourers are working longer than eight hours a day.
What about the wages paid those workmen?

The wages are low, but on the other hand those wages bring in more in the shape of substantial' comforts to the workers of Belgium than they do to the workers in Nova Scotia.
Furthermore, in regard to other conditions of work, I should like the hon. member to study certain tables which have been published by the International Labour Office showing the progress of ratifications of the treaty. He will find that Belgium stands high with respect to hours, unemployment, childbirth, night work (women), minimum age (industry), night work (young persons), and so on. When we come to Canada's part in regard to these matters, we find there is an absolute blank, so that the impression given by the hon. member opposite is far from being correct.
I am not going to say anything about reparations, to which reference has been made, exoept to state that one of the difficulties is that the countries paying reparations have had to lower their standards of living, and we are being adversely affected because of that. I would urge-
It is six o'clock.

I will close in a
word or two. I would say that undoubtedly any failure of a large industry of this kind will undoubtedly seriously affect the workers of Nova Scotia; indeed it will seriously affect the whole of Canada; but before assistance in any form whatever is given to this industry I would urge that certain conditions be laid down. The industry must be thoroughly reorganized and the interests of the workers in every respect thoroughly safeguarded.
Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. gentleman shall have leave to withdiaw his motion? Carried.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a few remarks on the question.

It being six o'clock I leave the chair.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
Mr. A. de WITT FOSTER (Hants-ICings): Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I had succeeded in catching your eye and arresting the attention of the House for a "brief moment, and I assure you it is not my intention to detain the House at any length in discussing this very important matter. It is a matter exceedingly important to the province of Nova Scotia, to the Maritime provinces, and I venture to suggest to the whole Dominion of Canada. It is important to the constituency which I represent, and that in the main is the first consideration which induces me to detain the House for a few moments in discussing some of the points that have been raised in the discussion this afternoon.
It is true that the steel industry is not located in either of the counties which I have the honour to represent in this House, but like so many of the industries of Canada the ramifications of which extend to the various portions of the Dominion, it is not surprising that this company and its success should have a marked influence upon conditions arising in my own constituency.
I said it was important to all the Maritimes. When one remembers that 25,000 people are employed in this industry in the province of Nova Scotia, and that one-fifth of the entire population are practically dependent upon it for their living, one sees at once the market for the products grown in the rest of the province which is here contained in the cities which are the very centres of the steel and coal industry. The apples that are raised in the Annapolis valley, many of them, find a market in New Glasgow and Sydney and various portions of Glace Bay, and in other coal, steel and iron centres. The products of the farm, butter and eggs, while they come into competition with other similar products, nevertheless have to find a portion of their market in these cities. In the winter time some of our men are engaged in the woods getting out pit props in the eastern part of Nova Scotia, and ties are obtained for laying in the various tracks of Besco's mileage. In

Dominion Iron and Steel
that way the ramifications of the industry can be seen to extend into the various sections and centres of our province, in fact, throughout the whole Maritime provinces.
It is on behalf of these people that those who have spoken from this side of the House have approached the consideration of this question. It is not from the point of view of defending a corporation. The corporation of Besco is personally, save in the by and large, unknown to me. By that I mean I have not had the pleasure of meeting either the president or the officers of the company.
