I have not had the opportunity to enter into an examination of their financial standing or status or of any of the intricate problems with which the company's officials alone would be familiar. I presume in that respect I am somewhat in the same position as the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), who inquired this afternoon why it was that we had not specifically placed before the House the exact conditions that mitigated against the success of this company. He alone of members on this side of the House, assuming for the moment the geographeial position rather than that of political distinctions, would have an opportunity of knowing what the problems of this company were and what requests they were making from the government. In general policy at any rate we are led to believe that the hon. member for Brandon has access to the demands which have been made upon the government, and it was with that idea in mind that I asked him the question I did this afternoon, and which he evaded answering. However, I find no fault with him for that, and I take this opportunity of thanking him for the interest he manifested, and for the promise he gave that in the consideration of this and other eastern difficulties we would have his consideration, and, I rather think I might say from his remarks, his support along certain lines, if not wholeheartedly, at least some support. I appreciate and gratefully acknowledge the proffered suggestion and support of the hon. member. I wish, however, that he might make a definite pronouncement that in matters affecting the east, as in those affecting the west, he would be willing to go as far with us as we have shown our willingness to go with him and those whom he leads in this House, in regard to legislation which has been brought forward for that particular section of the country.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mt. Woodsworth) rather led the House to think that we on this side were speaking in defence of the company, but as I pointed out a moment ago there is no hon. gentleman in this party Who has reason to 14011-2834
defend the particular policy of the officials of Besco. I have not heard that suggested, and I am sure it is not so; but we do have in mind the very serious condition which will result to the workers in those mines and to the people of the Maritime provinces in particular if a remedy is not provided. It does seem to me that if we had come here with the identical case which has been submitted to the government by the Besco officials and presented it to the House, we might then have been accused, and with some show of reason, of presenting a case in favour of the company itself. But we have not done so. In fact we have approached this question in an entirely non-partisan way, because we believe that when one of the major industries of this country is shaken to its very foundation and when a crisis is approaching it, the situation should not be made a political question to the extent of at least effecting no remedy and allowing such industry to come to grief.
Mention was made of the capitalization of Besco. I fail to see what that has to do with the matter, for the reason that we have been told by the Minister of Finance that up to the present time Besco had not paid any dividends on its second preferred nor yet on its common stock. Surely it cannot be claimed that in the bonds issued there was over-capitalization and that the property is not worth the value of the bonds. I fear it is default upon the bonds that will take place in the early summer rather than default upon any stock.
Mention was made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in discussing this question that the government had gone into the matter to a very considerable extent. According to the conversations which he repeated and the letters and telegrams which he read, they had had various conferences with the officials of Besco, and it seemed to me, if I gathered the proper deductions, that the reason why action had not been taken turned upon the non-receipt of a report called the Coverdale report, the officials of Besco claiming that the report in question was a private document for their own particular use, and the government maintaining that they could not act without having this report in their posj session. I venture to assume that there may be material in this report which it would not be wise for the public to know in view of the present serious situation. I feel certain, however, that the officials of Besco would be perfectly willing to produce this report for the examination of the members of the cabinet, on their assurance that the matter would be treated as confidential. In view of
Dominion Iron and Steel

the difficulties connected with the situation and the calamitous results that are likely to ensue, as has been pointed out and as is believed at least by the people of eastern Canada, the government should not hesitate, because of a technicality of that nature, to provide at least some of the suggested remedies which have occurred to them in the discussion of this problem, if not all that have been claimed by the management itself.
We were told that there were three phases of this question upon which a solution depended. One of these is the tariff. With that I do not propose to deal, because I am sure my views on that subject would not coincide with thpse of the government, and inasmuch as the tariff commission is already investigating the matter it seems to me that an interim report might very well be made by that commission to the government to aid them in arriving at proper conclusions. 1 have my own ideas as to what those conclusions ought to be; but I cannot speak for the commission, and the results I have in mind may be arrived at in a manner different from that which we on this side have been led to believe is the right and proper way. And so I say that so far as the tariff 13 concerned, if the government could secure such information as has been laid before the tariff commission, that in itself might help them to come to a conclusion upon the point.
The Minister of Finance dealt with the question of the claims urged by the company for certain moneys, and I am bound to say that his position in that regard seemed to me to be eminently fair, inasmuch as the moneys have been paid into the public treasury and, as the minister pointed out, only parliament itself could vote those moneys back again. With respect to other claims, they should be on a parity with the rest. As regards the government's position on these two matters I venture to say that very little fault can be found; but the fact remains that having taken that position and adhered to it, no relief can come so far as the ministry is concerned without bringing those matters to the attention of this House and laying before it some concrete proposition upon which it could act. It is that thought I had in mind with the desire of suggesting it to the minister.
The other point I had in mind was that relief might come to some of these industries through the medium of a bounty. Being a protectionist, as I announced on a previous occasion, I have no fault to find with the system of bounties, but they must be sparingly used and applied for proper purposes.

I remember reading a speech on the subject of bounties delivered in this House by the Hon. W. S. Fielding on December 14, 1909, in which the hon. gentleman made, as I believe, one of the most successful cases, if not the most successful, in favour of bounties that has ever been made in this House. In the course of that speech he pointed out that while the government had paid out some $13,000,000 in ten years to the steel industry in this country, yet in the various places where steel and iron were manufactured-[DOT] such as Sault Ste. Marie, Sydney, North Sydney, Sydney Mines, Glace Bay, New Glasgow and Hamilton-the increase in the customs duties alone at these points had been over $9,700,000, or less than $4,000,000 short of the entire amount which has been paid out in bounties. And from that he argued that in thus giving a stimulus to this industry, the producing power of the country had been increased, more wealth had been created, and as a consequence the people of the country were able to pay into the treasury almost as much as had been voted from it to this particular industry. Whether the subject of bounties is one which the government should consider is not for me to say; I merely point out that there is an argument to be advanced in favour of bounties, the most extreme kind of protection.
The main point of the whole matter, it seems to me, is that we ought not to allow this House to prorogue, we ought not to allow this debate to finish, until we have at least some indication that the government will take this matter into consideration and that if it is not done before the House closes they will do by order in council, if they can do it, what they have in mind for the benefit of this industry. We should be told that the government are willing to submit for the consideration of the House certain conclusions at which they have arrived for the benefit, indeed for the saving, of this industry. If we can judge from the remarks of hon. members to my left, I believe this House will be willing to give earnest and non-partisan consideration to this problem. I regard it one of the greatest Maritime problems, and with that statement I believe the ministry agrees.

It was not my intention to take part in this debate, and I would not have assumed the responsibility of continuing the debate past six o'clock, but since the hon. member who has just spoken assumed that responsibility, it may not be out of place for me to continue the discussion.
I do not propose to say anything about the

Dominion Iron and Steel
British Empire Steel Company itself-at least not that portion of the company's business which relates to steel-but by general consent it would seem that the coal interests are linked up with the steel business, and on that question I propose to make some very brief remarks.
When the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) was speaking I interjected a few remarks which the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) interpreted later as throwing some doubt upon the quality and availability of Nova Scotia coal. He quite correctly interpreted my remarks, and, speaking honestly, Mr. Speaker, there does seem to be some question as to the quality of Nova Scotia coal and its availability. By that I mean the cost at which that coal can be la:d at the pit's mouth. The right hon. leader of the opposition suggested to me that if I had a coal mine on my farm it would be better to dig that coal, and set my family digging it, than get it elsewhere. I should not like to give an unqualified consent to a proposition of that kind. It would depend altogether upon circumstances, and upon the spread between what it would cost me to dig that coal and what it would cost me to get it elsewhere. I was reminded of the story of a farmer who was travelling along the road with a tank of water. A stranger met him and asked him how far he was drawing the water. He said, " three miles." The stranger said, "Would it not be better for you to dig a well"? The farmer replied) to him, "Well, it is just about as far that way as the other way" , and I presume it would be sound protectionist doctrine to dig a well three miles deep instead of to draw water for the same distance. That is an extreme illustration, but after all does it not elucidate the point I wish to make, namely that we must give some attention to the question of cost when we are considering whether we will develop our own resources, whether we will dig our own coal or buy it elsewhere ?
There seems to be some question in the minds of many with reference to Nova Scotia coal. I made the statement this afternoon that there were some things I could not understand, and the hon. member for Pictou sarcastically remarked that there were many things I did not understand. That I am quite prepared to admit, and among them are the reasons advanced as to why a certain policy should be followed. Now the reason for not developing Nova Scotia coal is that Nova Scotia coal is not of equal quality to other coal used for the same purpose. On the other hand, when provincial rights are touched the
Maritime men stand up and declare that their coal is equal to any other, and they resent very keenly any statement to the contrary, as the hon. member for Pictou said in referring to the remarks made by the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke).

The hon. member
asserted two or three times this afternoon that Nova Scotia coal was of an inferior quality, and he attributed the statement to some particular individual or authority. I should like him to name that authority.
If the hon. member will call upon me privately I will tell him all I have in mind and the sources from which I have gained my information.

There is nothing
private about it.

Very well. We have had it brought before us that Nova Scotia coal is very much inclined to slack When the proposal is made that it be shipped up the St. Lawrence, they tell us it does not stand handling, and again that it does not stand banking.
Who says that?
That seems to be very generally conceded.
Give me one authority who makes that statement.

I might go further and
state the ejfact propositions that have been made to us. One of the reasons given for the adoption of certain policies was that Nova Scotia coal for certain purposes was not worth within $2 a ton of American coal. I shall be very glad to give the hon. member the information.
Now is the time.

The matter has been brought before some of the members here in such a way that I do not feel at liberty to give to the House all that was said to us on the question. Personally I have no objection to doing it, but there are other considerations which, at the present time, I feel under obligation to observe. So that it is a subject to which we endeavour to give consideration, and I am perfectly willing myself to give consideration to these questions. But when we are asked to endorse a certain policy we must know the facts. From my own observation there seems to be reason to believe that doubt can be thrown upon the quality of Nova Scotia coal, and not only upon the quality, but upon the cost of laying it at
Dominion Iron and Steel

the pit's mouth. A party of Progressive members visited Nova Scotia some years ago. We went down one of the coal mines in New Glasgow. We were told that that was the driest mine in Nova Scotia, and we were also informed that it was necessary to take out one ton of water for every ton of coal. Whether that is economical or not I do not know, but we are informed also that in some of the mines in Nova Scotia they had to elevate five tons of water for every ton of coal they took out. Then it would seem to be a fact that some of these mines are now extending out miles under the sea. Surely hon. members will admit the possibility that some of these mines-I will say only some of them-cannot be economically operated. If that is a fact, why not let us face it? It seems to be an admitted fact in regard to the mines in the Old Country. The newspapers tell us that some of the mines over there are in distress because they cannot be economically operated.
I understand the difficulties that confront us in a situation of that kind. It is not easy to move a population which has been built up around a certain industry, even when that industry can no longer be carried on economically. I appreciate that point and am prepared to give consideration to it.. But at least we want to know the facts, because it is only when we are face to face with the facts that we can hope to find a proper solution. The hon. member for Pictou did not do his case any good, but rather harm, when he took the leader of the* Progressive party to task for the statement he had made in reference to the quality of Nova Scotia coal and its availability. We were told, for instance, that some of the coal with which Nova Scotia has to compete, the Virginia coal, is loaded at the pit's mouth for about 90 cents a ton. One thing is certain, and that is that they are bringing large quantities of Virginia coal into the Maritime provinces We saw that when we were down there a year ago, and if the coal is of the quality they say it is, and if the mines can be operated as economically as they say they can be, then why the importation of Virginia coal into Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia itself? Let us know all the facts. If provincial pride conflicts with economic necessity they will have to put their provincial pride into their pockets and give the House and us from the west the fects so that we shall know how to face this question.
For my part, as I have already said, I am ready to give full consideration to policies that may seem to be necessary to meet the situ-

ation that has developed in the Maritime provinces. If it is true that their coal' is more given to slacking than some other coals, and that the cost both of laying the coal at the pit mouth and of transportation is unduly high, we will give consideration to those policies that are necessary to relieve that situation. Let us not have on the one hand evidence offered to us that would seem to throw doubt upon the quality of the coal, and on the other hand have men stand up in the House and find fault with those members who, trying only to arrive at the facts, make statements that meet with their disapproval. I may say again that the hon. member for Pictou did not do his cause any good but rather did it harm when he took the attitude he did in the House the other night.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one has less
reason to love the Dominion Coal Company or the Dominion Iron and Steel Company than I. I fought them at their formation for yeai-s and they followed me every time I contested a constituency. They had more money than I had and I went down. There is no doubt that the defeats I suffered in Nova Scotia were due to the expenditure of funds on the part of those associated with either the Dominion Coal Company or the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. But that is no reason why one should not approach the question with a fair and open mind.	.
The matter which is now up for consideration arises out of the fact that, on July 1 next, $5,159,000 of first mortgage bonds of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company will not pay their interest coupons, and that if the interest coupons are not paid on that date it is an absolute certainty that the interest will not be paid on $7,035,000 of consolidated mortgage bonds, interest on which is payable on September 1. Therefore it is perfectly clear that the Dominion Iron and -Steel Company is unable to operate with an operating profit sufficient to pay interest upon some twelve million dollars of its mortgage bonds. I understand the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) to say that the government at the present time has no suggestion of relief to make, but I would earnestly suggest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that this is a great industrial concern, and that the fact that it cannot pay interest upon its first and consolidated mortgage bonds for the coming year should not be clouded by the undoubted fact that in some of the stock, particularly the common stock, of that com-

Dominion Iron and Steel
pany, there may be water. With respect to the bonds one dollar of cash went in for every dollar of bonds outstanding. I think that is absolutely clear.
Mr. CAHI'LL:	Was there value there for
the bonds?

Value for the bonds and
much more. I am going to deal with that in a moment.
They are safe enough.

I do not know whether they are safe or not now; I am going to argue that point with the Prime Minister. If the announcement made by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company may be relied upon, this concern will be in the hands of a receiver during the summer months, and in the hands of a receiver they cannot operate unless the Prime Minister on behalf of this government will make some announcement which will induce the investment of sufficient funds to reconstruct that company on a sound and stable basis. If a receiver is appointed and no new announcement is made from the government, there is a fair possibility of that whole concern going down to wrack and ruin. If the Dominion Iron and Steel Company goes down during the summer months, if it is unable to induce capital to come in and assist in reconstructing the company on a sound financial basis, the Dominion Coal Company will go down with it, because the Dominion Coal Company cannot operate successfully unless it has a market for the coal which is now consumed by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. I think that is a fair statement. I am trying to keep within the limits.
What has brought this about? It is brought about by circumstances and conditions arising out of the war. I am not going to talk tariff for the moment; I am trying to place the facts as I see them before the Prime Minister and the members of his government. In 1913 we produced in Canada on an average every month 84,000 tons of pig iron. Last year we produced 48,000 tons. In 1913, we produced 87,000 tons of steel ingots and castings. Last year we produced 63,000 tons There has been a great diminution of production. To what is that due? It is due I think to lower costs of producing similar products in France and Belgium. The Minister of Finance said that there had been no large imporations from either France or Belgium, but I think I can say without fear of contradiction that during the past two or three years the price in Belgium and the price in France have governed the price in Canada. Therefore to produce at all in Canada the
Canadian companies have had to reduce their selling price to conform to the selling price in France and Belgium.
A great part of that iron which enters into production both in France and Belgium came out of the Ruhr during the Ruhr occupation.
A very considerable part of it comes out of Germany by way of reparations, and although France and Belgium have it at a certain price, in order to realize they have been selling their products and obtaining less return for the iron than they have actually credited Germany with in the matter of reparations. Two years ago this summer I was in France and England examining into some contracts in which a client of mine was interested for the sale of iron products coming out of the Ruhr to England. As a matter of fact the prices offered under those contracts were so low that producers of similar products in England would have been driven entirely out of employment at that time. The British government intervened and prevented those contracts from being carried out, because they held that it was a great injustice to producers in England to allow those cheaper goods to come in under the circumstances so as to destroy, for the time being, British industries. We can in this country secure those products temporarily from Belgium and France at les3 cost than that at which we can produce them profitably in this country. It is stated, and I have no doubt it is true, that reckoned in terms of the gold exchange the cost of production of iron and steel in both France and Belgium is half what it is anywhere in Canada. I do not think there is any doubt about that. Indeed, in a review by experts of the United States which I saw some time ago it was so stated. This is due partly to depreciated currency. Anyone who has examined into conditions in France and Belgium knows that reckoned in gold-because the prices at which these countries sell here are based upon that standard-wages have not increased proportionately to the depreciation of the franc in either country.
Is the hon. member sure of that fact?

I have it on the most reliable authority and I believe it to be true. Two years ago this summer I spent considerable time looking into the question with some of the best experts in England in connection with some contracts with which I was concerned. And I have seen large quantities of Belgian iron products coming into Canada. If I mistake not, last autumn I saw some iron for structural purposes being
Dominion Iron and Steel

landed in Montreal, and upon inquiry I ascertained that it was to be used in one of the government contracts. I cannot speak with personal knowledge of that, but I do know that a considerable quantity of this material is imported. The Canadian company to-day is obliged to meet the French and1 Belgian prices, and the cost of production has been so reduced in both these countries that their manufacturers can ship the product, pay the freight and the tariff as well, and sell cheaper than the Canadian producer can sell at a profit.
There is one other point to be considered. The duty on iron and steel has always been specific, and in 1913 it averaged, I think, pretty nearly 15 per cent; but with the prices now prevailing that specific duty reduced to ad valorem is only about 7 per cent. And that is without reference to any interposition on the part of the government; it is due simply to changing conditions of trade. The tariff against the French and the Belgian product is reduced one-half, and I suggest therefore that it is a fair matter for the consideration of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his government, apart altogether from any question of protection or free trade. There is invested in this industry some $500,000,000 in round figures-I have the specific figures somewhere if they are called for. It is for the government to consider whether that industry should not have at least the same protection as it enjoyed in 1913 under the conditions which then prevailed, and, if we are to have a specific duty, whether that duty should not be raised so as to give the same ad valorem protection as was afforded at that time.
Another important question arises, a question which must meet the Prime Minister and1 his advisers at every turn in dealing with a matter of this kind. We have in Canada a population of 9,000,000, stretching across the continent, with a population ol 112 or 114 millions to the south, producing the same things that we produce. The United States, with 5 per cent of the population of the world, produces 50 per cent of the entire output of the world's manufactures, This is according to the latest statistics I have seen. They can produce, owing to what is commonly called mass production, much cheaper than we can produce the same standard articles in Canada for a market of 9,000.000. The government must therefore decide, parliament must decide, whether in face of that competition we shall endeavour as best we can to safeguard Canadian industries m which there are large invest-

ments. We may be compelled to pay somewhat higher prices in Canada than those that obtain in the United States in respect of many of these products. Personally I think it is wise for the country to do so, and it is for the Prime Minister to decide that question. I understand there is a broad line of division, but we must face it if we are to preserve the financial, the industrial and the commercial integrity of the country.
One word more. I can quite understand that the Dominion Iron and Steel Cofnpany might not be prepared to submit the whole of the Coverdale report to the country, but I understand1 that they offered to produce it for the consideration of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). The Prime Minister and his colleague could have considered the report and decided whether there were certain matters which should be presented to the House and to the public and upon which they might base future action with regard to the company. There were, I know, certain other matters which might well be regarded as private and confidential and which it would not be fair to submit to their competitors. If I thought that the Dominion Iron and' Steel Company was not willing to have the government take from that report all matters really of public interest and which the government might reasonably require the House and the country to learn, and base upon these matters such action as they saw fit, I for one should feel reluctant to support the company. But I fancy there may have been some misunderstanding. I cannot understand that the representatives of the Dominion Iron and Steel would refuse to allow the government to take from the report all matters relevant and material to any decision which it might be called upon to make.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would it be unreasonable to ask that the minister of the crown representing the province concerned should have the same right as his colleagues to see that report?

I should think so. At one time under an order of the court I spent six months with twenty or thirty accountants in going through the books of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company from A to Z, and I think I knew them at that time as well as any person could after such an exhaustive investigation. I know they contain matters which should not be brought before the public and before their competitors; but there were other matters disclosed by those books which I think are very relevant, and in my view the

Dominion Iron and Steel
government has the right to have those facts in order that it may be in a position to render an intelligent judgment in regard to future action with respect to this company. That far I am with the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt my hon. friend, but may I ask him this question: Having gone through the books of the company, I think he referred a moment ago to its capitalization of $500,000,000; am I correct?

I was talking of all the companies engaged in the production of iron and steel products in Canada. I may have made a slip, but that is what I meant. Now I make this suggestion. It would be a most serious matter for Nova Scotia in particular, and possibly for Canada as a whole, if this undertaking in Cape Breton, Pictou and Cumberland, which may be termed a national undertaking, should go completely to the wall. I think it would be impossible to obtain the fresh capital necessary to place it on a basis where it could operate to a moderate extent, let alone to the full capacity of the plant, unless the government of the country announces some stable policy with regard to the iron and steel production of Canada. I do not want to put this offensively, but I say that company will go into the hands of a receiver unless there is some assurance that the industry will be safeguarded in a manner in which it is not now safeguarded against this foreign competition, and in that event, as a practical man, I think it would be impossible to obtain the new capital necessary to carry it on, on even the most conservative basis.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend seeks to place responsibility on the government of this country. Does he recognize no
responsibility on the part of the government of the province directly concerned?

Quite so, but so far as I can see, there is no announcement that the government of the province of Nova Scotia could make under present conditions which would create the confidence necessary in the public mind to secure the requisite fresh capital for the reconstruction of that company and the re-establishing of that industry. That was my point. I do not wish any unpleasant inference to be drawn from what I am saying; I simply want to state the facts because I recognize the government must take the lead. The responsibility ultimately will depend of course on the action of the parliament of Canada, but under present conditions it seems to me the government must take the lead. Here is a great industry being disrupted and
going to ruin, and unless the government acts very speedily I am afraid there will be no possibility of the redemption of that industry within the next few years. That is my sincere view. I am putting my own point of view before the Prime Minister, I am not endeavouring to throw any partisan prejudice into it at all, but I am simply trying to state the case to him with perfect frankness, because upon him really as the leader of the government there rests a very grave responsibility. Although I represent a constituency in Quebec and as a Conservative am opposed to him politically, personally I would go a long, long way to support any reasonably effective action that he and his government might take to save this industry from ruin.

Mr. Speaker, as a protectionist I have been very much impressed by the statement made by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) this afternoon that he and his friends would do what they could to support the government in applying a remedy to this situation. Let me suggest to the House what may prove to be a practical solution. Public ownership as applied in the province of Ontario to the distribution of power and light is of its kind one of the most marvellous enterprises I know of on the American continent. It is a great financial success, and to-day I am glad to say it has excited the envy of private enterprises competing against it.
Now, to my mind what Nova Scotia ought to do as a way out of this trouble is to handle the problem by way of public ownership- pool the leading mines, devote them to the production of electric energy near the pitheads and distribute that energy all over 9 p.m. the province for power and light, and ship the balance of the product of those mines to Quebec and Ontario for fuel. In this way the coal industry of Nova Scotia would be put on its feet, it would supply power and light for the province, and it would also supply fuel for Ontario and Quebec.
Now then, if the steel industry of Nova Scotia had the assurance of coal at cost, or very nearly at cost, produced from the pick of the mines that had been pooled, that of itself would be an encouragement to that industry. Then if the company had to be reorganized, capital would be forthcoming for the reconstruction of the steel industry. That is what we want to see. If they can have, as they have, a great steel industry in the United States, I say we can have a great steel
Dominion Iron and Steel

industry in this country. Evidence came out this afternoon that to-day the Americans are the greatest producers of steel at the cheapest price, and they sell it all over the world. They are the most protectionist country on the face of the globe.
Now, Mr. Speaker, by adopting this western principle of pooling the best of the coal mines in Nova Scotia we would get coal almost at cost; the coal industry would flourish, and it would enable us to insist that the men who work the mines get decent pay and decent houses to live in. That is another progressive idea, but it is worth while considering. This summer if we are to have a commission investigate the industries of the Maritime provinces, I should like to see it take up the coal and steel industries on the lines I have suggested. I am, of course, only stating it crudely to-night, but I am confident that in my suggestion there is contained the key to the solution of some of these Maritime grievances, for it will enable the miners to be paid good wages, and by the establishment of coking plants in Ontario and Quebec we can handle the coal of Nova Scotia, supply the fuel wants of the central provinces and get the advantage of all the by-products incident to the coking process. That will open a new vista for the people in the Maritime provinces. I am not going to take up any more time, but I just throw that out as a supplementary proposal. I think the government have 'been impressed by the debate this afternoon and will listen to the various suggestions that have been made, and I believe they will see that it is their duty to do something in the way of coming to the relief of Nova Scotia if this crisis of which we are told to-day really does impend, because it would mean a great injury to a great industry that we have in this country. If we want to go into the steel business, we must go into it in much the same way as the United States have done. We must encourage it, and perhaps the best way to encourage it was suggested here tonight, and as the Prime Minister says, probably the provinces ought to do something too. But probably the best relief would be by the bounty system. I know nothing that is better calculated to encourage an industry in a country than the bounty system, backed by the province and the Dominion. But some duty is on the government, so far as I can see, after hearing the debate here this afternoon, and is incumbent also, I think, on the province and on this House and the 
people of Canada, and especially the people of Quebec and Ontario, to take their coal from the Maritime provinces instead of sending their money to the coal mines of the United States.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Naturally, Mr. Speaker,
I am very deeply interested in this question and in the discussion which has taken place to-day. I want to commend my colleagues from Nova Scotia on the very fair and reasonable manner in which they have presented for the consideration of the House the problems that face us in Nova 'Scotia in regard to the steel industry. The discussion, however, has gone very far afield. We have drifted off into the consideration of whether Nova Scotia coal was good or bad, and into coal questions generally. All these matters have no relation at all to the vital issue before us. There is only one issue before us-small only having regard to all the other questions that have been referred to this afternoon and this evening, but in itself very vast and important.
Intimation was made to the government by representatives of the British Empire Steel Corporation that the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, one of their subsidiaries, was in such a position that they feared a receiver would have to be appointed. The reason they thought that course would have to be taken was on account of the information contained in the report of special accountants, known as Coverdale and Colpitts, who had made full and complete inquiries into the workings of the company and of all its subsidiaries. I happened to be present with my two colleagues, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), when the president of the company conveyed that information to us, and I asked him what did he propose as a remedy. There were only two proposals that he made: first, that there should be a rearrangement of the law in regard to goods coming from countries where there was a depreciated currency; and secondly, he made an argument in favour of a bounty being granted upon coal that was used in the production of steel. He pointed out, by way of illustration, that the Steel Company of Canada and the Steel Company at the Soo, when they imported coal into Canada and used that coal in the manufacture of steel were entitled to receive and did receive a rebate from the government of 99 per cent of the duty that they had paid on the coal when it entered. Therefore, he argued that Nova Scotia should get a bounty of 50 cents upon

Dominion Iron and Steel
every ton of coal that entered into the production of steel. That would mean a .bounty of $2 a ton on every ton of steel. I stated to the president of the British Empire Steel Corporation that I could hardly see the logic of his proposition. In the one case you were rebating duties to companies importing coal, and you were not giving any subsidy at all, but in the other case you proposed to go into the treasury and give a subsidy of $2 a ton on every ton of steel manufactured out of Canadian coal, and that the proposal was one that we would have to consider very carefully. In view of the conditions which he said existed in the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, as disclosed of this report of Coverdale and Col-pitts, the government came to the conclusion that in order to have t'he full and proper information before us, in order to ascertain first, what was the cause of existing conditions, and secondly, what we ought to do, we could not move intelligently unless we had that report. I think the House will agree with me that that was a reasonable and proper proposal, and so my hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) conveyed that information to the president of the company.
Hon. gentlemen who were here this afternoon have followed the correspondence which took place, in which Mr. Wolvin took the position that he would not produce the report. Finally, at a conference on Friday last he intimated to the Prime Minister and my colleague the Minister of Finance that he would produce the report for their private consumption only, and that they should not be permitted to communicate even to their colleagues in the government what was in the report. Now that is naturaly a very unreasonable position. Every hon. gentleman who has parliamentary or governmental experience knows that under the oath of office that every privy councillor takes, there are at all times important matters of confidential character which all members of the government have to keep secret in the public interest. We never thought of suggesting that the report should be given to us for the purpose of being thrown open to the public or anything of that kind, but simply and solely for the purpose of enabling us to know the cause of the present conditions, and what was the best remedy-^-because enough was said, and enough has been said in addresses to the shareholders of this company, to indicate that this firm of accountants did make certain findings and also certain recommendations as to the future.
The position of the government is this: We feel we are entitled, before we come to any
policy in regard to the matter, to a perusal of that report. It might be found necessary that certain portions of the report should be given to the House and the country in justification of any action we might propose to take or of any policy we propounded. I am sure that no hon. gentleman with any sense of responsibility would say that this government could act until we have before us the facts contained in that report. We are not insensible to the present position of the company; we appreciate the grave consequences that would follow to the province by the sea if this steel industry should fail, or as my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) said, be ruined. The consequences would be serious not only to the section where this industry is located, but to all the other industries throughout the province. We are prepared to give the fullest and most sympathetic consideration to any proposition that can be made, and will endeavour to devise proposals in order that what is said to be impending may be averted. But we do think, and we submit to the House, that the president of the British Empire Steel Corporation should allow us to examine that report in order that, being acquainted with the facts, we migjht know what to do.

I shall take but a bare three or four minutes, to reply to a remark made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) as to the wages paid in the steel industries in Europe as compared with the wages paid in the same industries on this side. During his remarks, after he had mentioned that there were laws in Belgium forcing workmen to work eight hours per day, I asked him what about wages, and while he admitted that the cash wages were higher on this side of the water, at the same time he said that the wages they received in Belgium purchased as much goods as the amount of wages received over here. Now in 1924 I discussed this wage question in the House with the then Minister of Labour, Mr. Murdock; the then member for Red Deer, who is also the sitting member for that constituency (Mr. Speakman) backed me up, and we asked the Minister of Labour to put on record the wages paid over there as compared with the wages paid here. He said that he had these figures after a very thorough investigation had been made by the British Ministry of Labour. These figures are not figures obtained by the Canadian Ministry of Labour, by the Conservative party, by the Liberal party, the Progressive party, or the Labour

Dominion Iron and Steel
party, but figures obtained by the British Ministry of Labour after full investigation. And they are not cash wages, they are what are called "real" wages, that is the cash turned into food, clothing, rent and so forth. I have here the report issued by the Canadian Minister of Labour, Mr. Murdock, on May 20, 1924, and recorded in Volume III, page 2339 and subsequent pages, of Hansard of that year. Mr. Murdock points out that these are figures of the British Ministry of Labour. I mention that because he himself points that out. He mentions various lines of work in Europe and the real wages obtained by the workers in those occupations. The statement shows the wages paid in Belgium, France, Germany, England, in any of the European countries from Austria on the east right west to the British islands. It is pointed out that in no one of these countries does the rate of wages come within one-half to one-fifth of the rate of wages paid in Canada. I am going to give a couple of instances which bear out the statement, and I shall take the engineering trades, which are more or less related to the industry we have been discussing to-day-that is the iron and steel industry. I will only mention a few of the cities but I desire to draw special attention to Brussels, Paris, New York and Ottawa. I imagine most hon. members will realize it is important to understand what real wages are. That point arises because of an argument made on a former occasion by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). I repeat that real wages are wages converted into food, clothing, and shelter, the necessaries of life.
What is the index number?

In London the index number is taken as 100. The figures for the engineering trades are as follows:
London	 100
Amsterdam	 108
Berlin	 57
Brussels	 73
And it was of Belgium that my hon. friend was speaking.
Christiania	 104
Madrid	 83
New York	 162
Ottawa	 196
Paris	 58
Prague	 54
Stockholm	 79
Vienna	 62
Warsaw	 61
I will repeat just here these four: Brussels, 73; Paris, 58; New York, 162; and Ottawa, 196. It will be seen that the figure for Ottawa

was four times what the Paris figure was, and almost three times the Brussels figure. These are figures dealing particularly with the engineering trades that are most closely related to the industry we have been discussing to-day.
Oh, no.

These trades are just as
closely related as any trades that are contained in the same report. They deal with fitters, iron moulders, pattern makers, and turners-occupations, I think, closely related to the iron and steel industry.
No.

These trades have a great deal to do with the iron and steel1 industry; they are the closest to it that I could find for the purposes of illustration. What does my hon. friend say the closest occupation would be, that of men engaged in foundries?

I think my hon. friend
will find: that none of the trades he mentions have to do with the British Empire Steel Corporation's problem.
What he said was that they were as high as they were in Sydney, Nova Scotia.	[DOT]

My hon. friend is right, the member for Winnipeg North Centre did say that. But in this record the wages are not given for Sydney, Nova Scotia. However, I have no reason for thinking that the wage rate is materially lower in Nova Scotia than it is in Ottawa. I presume the Ottawa figure is a composite figure for the whole of Canada, although I do not know whether that is actually the case. But the fact remains, as shown from figures compiled after careful investigation by the British Ministry of Labour, that the real wages-whether in the British islands or any other of the Continental Countries-are materially lower than the wages paid in Canada.
Motion withdrawn.
The House resumed from June 11 consideration in committee of Bill No. 189, to provide for a loan to the Harbour Commisisoners of Montreal-Mr. Cardin-Mr. Duff in the chair.

The other night the committee passed the different clauses of the bill with the understanding that I should give further explanations in regard to the report
supplied to the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) with respect to the purchase of certain properties needed for the landing of the Montreal bridge on the island of Montreal. 1 must state that the harbour commissioners primarily considered it would be more advantageous to effect the purchase of these various properties by private sale, if at all possible, rather than by expropriation proceedings or any other method. The engineers, when preparing the estimates of the cost of the bridge, went into the valuations of the properties which it might be necessary to acquire for the approaches. These figures prepared by the engineers have been checked by the representative of the city of Montreal, Mr. Terrault- who, as a matter of fact, represents the city of Montreal on the advisory board which has been formed by the harbour commission, for the special purpose of advising the commission in all matters concerning the bridge. On this advisory board is also found the name of Mr. Vallee. He is an engineer of the provincial government, who supervises the construction of all bridges built by that government. Mr. Vallee is a member of the advisory board with Mr. Terrault. All these figures were also checked by Mr. Beique, real estate man in Montreal, a man of experience in his trade. They were carefully gone over by Mr. Browne, a man having a thorough knowledge of real estate in Montreal, in fact I think he has been in the real estate business in that city for thirty-five years. The engineers' estimates regarding the cost of the acquisition of the property necesary for the approaches of the bridge in Montreal at first placed it at $1,400,000. Later on, after further examination, it was found' by Mr. Beique, that the amount necessary to purchase said property would probably be $1,645,000. The valuation as given out by Mr. Browne, was $1,560,000. On account of certain difficulties encountered with the proprietors of very large real estate properties the course of the landing was somewhat changed. A suggestion was made that there should be a change because the original plan involved the expropriation of property of very large value. It was in fact discovered that it would cost too much to expropriate this property at the price asked by the proprietors, therefore a change was made in the course to be followed by the approaches and the estimates were accordingly reduced to $1,184,800. Judging by the progress made up to the present in the buying of the property, the commissioner and those working for him in this connection are under the impression that the whole expropriation will not cost more than $1,000,000. Obligations have been undertaken

Montreal Harbour Commission
for about $750,000, and this represents much over one-half of the value of the property which will be required for the approaches; in fact, it is nearly three-quarters of all the real estate which it will be necessary to secure for that purpose.
In the sworn declaration which was read by the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) the other night, the civic valuation of five properties is given, probably based on the valuation of these properties to determine the price at which they should be bought. According to my information, the civic valuation is never taken as a basis for the valuation of property. In fact the city of Montreal has made numerous expropriations and particularly, in one instance for what is known as the boulevard Saint-Joseph. Expropriation proceedings were carried on, and it can :be fully established to-day that the price that was paid in these expropriations was nearly five times the amount of the civic valuation in that locality. The same thing has happened in other instances. For example, in the expropriation of land needed for the Windsor Street station, the Canadian Pacific Railway paid as high as $22 a foot for property which was never assessed at such a high price. The same thing occurred in many cases in the expropriations carried on by the same company on Notre-Dame street. On the occasion of the sale by auction of the old fire station on St. Catherine street, near Bleury, which was sold for $61.75 a square foot, the assessment was one-third of this amount. The old High School was sold at auction for $1,385,000, and the assessment was about one-third of that amount. The property at the corner of Laurier avenue and St. Lawrence boulevard was sold at $12.50 a foot, five times the city assessment. In fact the' city valuation has never been taken as a basis for determining the price which is to be paid for properties to be expropriated.
I will now give the committee the information given me' by those who are negotiating for the harbour commission in trying to acquire property by private sale. Take the first case mentioned in the sworn declaration, P-31, P-32, P-33, this property has a frontage of 127 feet on Notre Dame street, 124 feet on Craig street and 31 feet on Delorimier avenue and is entirely built upon. It has a frontage on three streets, it is shallow in depth and contains an area of about 5,000 feet. The first price asked for the property was $75,000. According to my information, this property had been valued' by Mr. Julian and Mr. Chausse

at a price of $100,000. There had been numerous interviews with the proprietor and the first option which had been obtained was for $60,000. It was afterwards discovered that half of the property belonged to a man named Gilbert residing in Belgium. After negotiations the property was bought for the sum of $45,000, which was a very favourable price indeed, because in the same locality Molson's, the brewers, had paid the sum of $10 a foot for a similar pietce of land, and on top of this, there is the question, of the buildings. Therefore, according to my information and the representations which have been made, the price which has been paid for this property is quite correct. To show that we did not rely too much upon the civic valuation, I may say that Mr. Bernier, who made the sworn declaration, gives the civic valuation of this property as $22,500 and he says,:	My own
valuation would be $35,000." That shows that he doe's not himself place very much reliance upon the civic valuation of the property. Has he more experience than others? Is he entitled to more credit for his valuation? Nobody can say, but according to information given already and prices paid for properties situated in the same locality, I think we are right in concluding that thq price of $45,000, paid for a property covered by buildings and situated iu practically the centre of the eastern part of the city of Montreal, is not very high.
As regards property P-491, it has a frontage of 80 feet on Delorimier avenue by 120 feet deep. It is only 42 feet from St. Catherine street, and it is practically St. Catherine street frontage. If the owners of the property fronting on St. Catherine street had acquired this property, we would have had to pay $12 a foot for it. According to the ratio of values, this property is worth $9 a foot. The owner has been asking $8, and the price paid by a representative of the harbour commission is $6.50 a foot. The civic valuation of the property is $18,500, and Mr. Bernier says:	"My own valuation would be
$38,600." According to the sale of similar properties in the vicinity, the price which has been paid, namely $78,000, is fair and reasonable, and even a low price. We are told by men of experience that if we had gone through the ordinary expropriation procedure we would have paid a higher price for this property, in addition to the cost of expropriation, and we would have incurred all the delays of such a procedure.
As regards property P-492, it has a frontage of 36 feet on St. Catherine street and is within 40 feet of Delorimier avenue on the

Montreal Harbour Commission
transfer corner. It has only a depth of 42 feet, all built upon with a meat and sausage business fully equipped, doing a trade amounting to $120,000 a year. The owner asked at first $65,000 for the property, good-will, loss of business, removal of fixtures, and an ice plant installed which would thus be rendered useless and which had cost $12,000. The commission has paid $22,500 for the property itself, and they have allowed the sum of $18,500 for the loss of his business, removal of fixtures- Loss of trade, and so on, which amount certainly could have been obtained by the proprietor in any expropriation proceedings. Mr. Bernier gives the civic valuation of this property as $9,500 and says that his own valuation would be $25,000. This shows once more that the civic valuation can not be of any help in determining the value of properties.
As regards property P-493, Mr. Bernier gives the civic valuation as $48 000 and he says that his ora valuation would be $75,000 and that he is informed that the said property has been bought privately by the harbour commission for the sum of $125,000. This is not correct, because the said property is being expropriated; it has not yet been bought, and the price will be determined under expropriation proceedings.
As regards property P-294, it has a frontage of 46 feet on St. Catherine street, and it contains an area of over 3.000 square feet. It is fully built on with a brick building. The price originally asked by the proprietor was $75,000, which was entirely out of the question. By gradually negotiating with the owner, the commission got the price down to $47,500, and the deal was finally put through at $44,500. The building cannot be erected for $30,000, not to speak of the cost of the ground. This building is valued at $35,000 by the same party who valued P-492 at $25,000, although the land is double the size and the building is a brick building, three storeys and basement. Even basing the value on the same valuation, the area being double, the man should have valued this property at not less than $50,000, plus a certain amount on account of the difference in value between the north and the south side of St. Catherine street and the difference in value between a brick building and a wooden building.
I am afraid that some people may have been disappointed because they have been deprived of an opportunity to make some money out of the purchase of certain properties which were needed for the building of the approaches to the bridge. My information goes so far as to permit me to state
that the man, whose name is mentioned on the certificate of research which was produced or read by the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) the other day, has been trying to get in touch with the proprietors of a certain number of properties in order to act as their agent and has even promised certain proprietors a large profit in the case of the property being expropriated by the harbour commission. To show that the purchases which have been made are really advantageous, I may say that one of the proprietors agreed to give a Mr. Julien, probably the man whose name is mentioned on the certificate of research, authority to sell his property or to act as his agent. He signed a document setting forth the conditions upon which he was prepared to part with the property. He fixes the price at $12,000, and he says to the agent in effect, "If you cannot get $12,000 you will receive no fee for your services in this transaction." I am informed that said agent asked the harbour commission the sum of $14,000 for the same property which has been acquired by the commission, through its own agent, for $9,500. This is one illustration of the good work which the commission is doing.
Attention has been called to the fact that, according to the certificate of research, no mention has 'been made of the prices at which these properties have been acquired. In the matter of price, the only indication that appears is the phrase, "One dollar and other considerations". May I observe that a general statement of this kind is nothing new. Wherever properties are purchased on an extensive scale, it is the practice to omit from the deeds any reference in direct terms to the price paid, inasmuch as it would be to the disadvantage of the company or the person making the purchase or, in the case of the crown, the expropriation to have it made public just what was .paid in any instance. The price is kept secret between the buyer and the seller, and this avoids any possibility of exorbitant demands being made subsequently for other properties. This is the procedure which, as a general rule, has been followed in connection with expropriations.
It has been pointed out further that apparently ail these properties have been purchased in the name of one particular individual. There is nothing extraordinary about this. We are trying to secure these properties privately, and when they have all been acquired it will be easier to transfer them to the harbour commission if they have been

I have no information in

My information is that a

Last week my hon. friend told' us that the city of Montreal was paying one-third and the province of Quebec another third. I think he must be mistaken, for as I understand it the legislature of the province has passed legislation on behalf of 10 p.m. the city of Montreal and on its own behalf that each will be responsible to the extent of $150,000. The other night the minister told us that this



Montreal Harbour Commission
bridge will cost $15,000,000. I do not suppose he will get the money at less than 5 per cent, or an annual charge of $750,000, and if the city of Montreal 'and the province of Quebec are to ibe called upon to pay only $300,000, the Dominion will be responsible to the extent of $450,000 annually. So if we allow this bill to go through we will be called upon to pay* a great deal more than we originally agreed to be responsible for, the first arrangement having been for a contribution of a third by the city of Montreal, another third by the province of Quebec, and1 the remaining third by the harbour board through the Dominion.
The minister is good enough to acknowledge that the evidence I produced the other night was quite correct. Therefore -before he asks us to proceed with this bill I hope he will get some definite information on the points I have referred to, and if he does, I can assure him there will be no delay in passing this measure so far as I am concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is my duty, in view of the question that has been raised with regard to the price of lots, and that has been dealt with by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to say some Words in his support. My own position is this, and I took this position in the campaign, that I was reluctant to see the bridge added on as a part of the harbour works of Montreal. We in Montreal regard the harbour -works as a great national undertaking, and if they cannot be justified as a great national undertaking they cannot, in imy opinion, be justified at all. As a national undertaking they must be kept clear of any shade or shadow of wrongdoing, any shade and shadow of graft or fraud. When it was represented to me, therefore, as a member from one of the Montreal constituencies, that a higher price had been paid with regard to those lots which have been dealt with specifically to-night by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I made the most careful examination that I could to ascertain the- facts, and I am in duty bound to say that I think that the purchases of those lots are free from any wrongdoing, and that the facts which I obtained after a careful inquiry are in entire accord with the explanation made here tonight by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I am dealing now specifically with lots P-31, 32, 33, 491, 492, 493 and 494. In the exercise of their discretion they may have paid a higher price than they possibly should have paid. It may have been that

by closer bargaining they could have taken a few thousand dollars off the price, but I will say that, having done everything I could in the way of inquiring and investigating whether there was any shade or shadow of fraud or wrongdoing in connection with those lots, I became convinced as an independent member of this House that there was nothing of the sort.

What about the old
lots?
They were not reported to me, and I do not know what lots were bought.

There were a quarter
of a million dollars' worth.

In the reports that were
made to me, it was these lots I have mentioned that were specifically referred to as matters that were open to debate. With regard to the others, I do not know. But I will say this, that in connection with the Montreal harbour works I think the accounts of that body should be audited from year to year by the Dominion government auditor. I do not think that is a matter that should be open solely and exclusively to a private auditing by the auditor who is engaged and is under the sole direction and control of the harbour commissioners. I think that change should be made.
There is no doubt that if one were to tell the truth-and I dislike to say it for fear of casting suspicion where no suspicion might lie-in connection with the contracts for the construction of the bridge in all its ramifications there has been a very great deal of gossip in the city of Montreal and a great deal of suspicion aroused as to the way in which those contracts were placed. Yet I am bound to say this:	I have been as persistent in trying to ascertain -the facts as a member could be, and I have not yet been able to find any fact that would warrant me making any charge against that commission. But I would be satisfied, and I am sure the citizens of Montreal would be better satisfied, if the accounts of that board were audited by the Auditor General or one of his representatives.
There is one other matter, and then I am done. In order that the commission may carry out its work as a great national work, I do not think the board of commissioners should be entirely changed with every change of government. The very fact that each succeeding government accepts the resignations of all the commissioners then in office and appoints an entirely new -body of commissioners from those of its own political

Montreal Harbour Commission
faith-from, if I might use a word that was allowed this afternoon by Mr. Speaker, its own henchmen-tends to discredit the work of the commission in the eyes of many of the people of Canada. If another government does ever come into office, or if a vacancy should occur in the present board of commissioners, I trust that the government will see that one member of that commission is nominally of the political faith of the opponents of the government. There is no reason why the government, being responsible for the work, should not have a majority on the commission, but it would give just a bit more confidence in' the commission if there ' was a minority on it representing the old regime. The board would then carry on always with a majority representing the government, who have the responsibility, but ' with at least one member of the old regime who knows what has been done and who would act as a. binding link between the two successive boards.

The west is vitally
interested in this harbour. It supplies . primarily the products from which the tolls are exacted that ensure the payment of the interest upon the securities that are emitted by the board and guaranteed by the government of Canada. It is not conducted, or 'should not be conducted, as a money-making enterprise. The harbour board is the creature of statute, a statute of this parliament. It issues securities; we pay them the money, and we have not yet any control over that expenditure. The Public Accounts committee of this House may not examine those accounts. We may not appoint a firm of auditors to audit them. That is the law at the moment. During the last session of parliament a large sum of money was voted for the construction of a bridge at Montreal. We are now being asked to vote the large sum of $12,000,000 for harbour purposes. It is true that we get for that $12,0100,000, securities which are issued by the harbour board, and those securities doubtless will have the interest paid upon them regularly. But I can say this to the Minister of Marine and to the Prime Minister, there is abroad in western Canada the idea that this harbour board's affairs are not conducted as they should be, that this country should have the right to audit those accounts in order that the rates charged might, if possible, be reduced and thereby render the charges on the shipment of grain from western Canada to the markets of the world cheaper than they, are now. That is the impression that prevails. There was, for instance, in one of the news-14011-
papers-it was carried as a despatch in many of the newspapers- last fall during the time of the election a very disconcerting paragraph. It indicated that the expenses of the election were being paid out of the funds that were derived out of these transactions. Now that is calculated to have a very injurious effect.
