Will my hon.
friend make a charge to that effect?

No, but I will tell you
what I am coming to. It is too late this session, but if I am here next session I am going to ask for a commission or parliamentary committee to investigate the operations of the harbour board for reasons that I am going to state. Those reports, I say, were circulated throughout western Canada and they found credence in many minds. There is one way in which this impression can be removed, and that is by a full, free and thorough audit by competent men of the accounts of the board, or by the submission of its accounts to the Public Accounts committee of Canada.
Let us look at this question of acquiring land. Land acquired by a public body is, of course, capable of being acquired by expropriation or by private treaty. I do not know what the law of Quebec may be, but in the other provinces, of whose laws I have some knowledge, it is customary to file a plan, and to vest the property, under the Public Works Act of Canada, or under the Railway Act, either in the railway or in the crown, as the case may be. Then there i3 a procedure whereby the price can be settled before a judicial tribunal or before a board of arbitration. But if private negotiations are carried on without the plan being filed, in ninety-nine cases out of one hundred the price paid would be and is excessive. In this instance the minister has been speaking to-night of expropriations, yet I find, after listening to his remarks, that in many instances there was nc such thing as expropriation. What happened was that in a number of cases they proceeded to negotiate by private treaty for the acquisition of lands that were used for the rights of way to this bridge on either side. Now, had a plan been filed and, to use a term in vogue in United States very largely, the land been condemned by the filing of the plan, then the price to be paid would be settled in one of the manners I have indicated. In this instance the proceedings have apparently been carried on by private negotiation or treaty, with the result, the minister asserts, that substantial sums of money had been saved. May I point out to him that the filing of the plan and the condemnation of the land, and expropria-

Montreal Harbour Commission
tion proceedings are What should be done under the law in all cases where the people of Canada are finding the money and a body over which they have no direct jurisdiction is spending it. I submit this axiom with respect to a matter of this kind: No public body that derives its moneys from this parliament should be permitted to carry on its operations except by strict regard to the law, which means that when property has to be acquired it should be acquired by condemnation and by expropriation in the manner provided by law. I submit that to the minister for his consideration.
I said a moment ago that grave suspicions were aroused because of articles that were circulated in the public press, not in one paper but in the public press generally, with respect to the relationship of the construction of these harbour works to the elections. If it were not at this time of the session I would make this motion:
That the accounts of the harbour board be referred to the Public Accounts committee for the purpose of enabling them to be investigated.
One should not make rash promises, for life is uncertain, but I do think that if I were privileged to be in this House another session I should make such a motion in the interest of western Canada. As a matter of fact there should be no necessity for such a motion; such a provision should be made by statute. It should be part of the law that where this country finds the capital sum for great public ports amounting to forty and fifty millions of dollars, as in t'he case of the city of Montreal, the expenditure of that money should be subject to the scrutiny of the representatives in parliament of the people most affected. I know of no part of this Dominion that is more interested in the harbour of Montreal than western Canada; and if these moneys are not expended with the most scrupulous care, with the most exacting care, with respect to every dollar that is obtained, it follows that the tolls that are imposed for the use of the harbour facilities will not be as low as they otherwise would be, and as a result of that western Canada will suffer. I admire greatly the harbour facilities in Montreal but I find great difficulty in understanding why we are now asked for $12,000,000 while at the same time we are talking of providing further accommodation at Hudson bay that will limit the [DOT]use of those facilities. In addition to limiting the use of the facilities at Montreal there is this also to be borne in mind: We have created a harbour board at Vancouver. Notwithstanding the harbour facilities that are being created on the Pacific we are now being

asked for $12,000,000 additional for Montreal when much of the grain traffic that used to flow to Montreal is now going to Vancouver. I can recollect the first shipment of grain that ever went from Vancouver through the Panama canal; I happened by accident to be associated with the enterprise conducting it. That is not so very long ago, but I have seen that traffic steadily develop and increase until there are now many million bushels of grain going from Vancouver to Europe through that canal. To the extent to which those facilities are used, to that extent there is a less demand made upon the facilities of Montreal. The [DOT] Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) may shake his head, but that carries no conviction. I know whereof I speak; I happen to know the facts with respect to this matter and it is not a matter of imagination. I had to do with the first cargo that went by the route in question.
There is one further question to be considered in relation to this matter. American grain is being sent through our ports. That is not an unmixed blessing. Some people say, "Expand your facilities in order that you may get more American traffic". But we have had our grain in western Canada held up because our facilities were being used by American grain. That is not hearsay either, that is a matter of record. Now if we are going to increase these facilities for the purpose of1 offering them to American grain and American commodities, thereby prejudicing t'he right to move our own commodities, then the less we do of it the better. However, the important point is the passing of the grant of $12,000,000.
I have given a little more than ordinary business consideration to the harbour of Montreal and its accounts. I have given some little attention to its cold storage facilities, to the charters of railway companies and others with respect to that harbour. I have studied with some little degree of care the various transactions that have taken place by which the present condition has been arrived at. I have seen the votes of this parlaiment last year. I am now called upon as a member of this House to express my approval or disapproval of this vote and I wholly disapprove of it at this moment. I wholly disapprove of it, first because I have no adequate and proper information vouched for by the auditors of this country, the shareholders or owners of these facilities in the ultimate analysis, that will enable me to say that the tolls charged are just and reasonable tolls having regard to the just and reasonable charges that should be made against that harbour. Secondly, I have not had presented to me any evidence that would warrant me in agreeing to a vote of

Montreal Harbour Commission
twelve millions at this moment, having regard to the condition of this country. If the movement of grain and other products westward, and the movement of products from Europe through the Panama canal to Vancouver for distribution on the prairie-that is the return cargoes-are to increase as they have, and if the Prince Rupert monument-I call it the monument-is to bear the inscription which was originally intended, obviously these facilities would not be so greatly required. But if indeed it is to be, as it now is, a monument to political necessity and business incapacity, then these facilities may be required. But when you think of that great property being rented for $100 per annum, one can readily understand the circumstances which should bring a blush of shame to the cheek of every Canadian, one can understand why parliament is asked to vote money for this purpose. But I go further and say that if I have the opportunity, I shall certainly demand, in the interests of western Canada, that the accounts of that harbour board are no longer left in the hands of a political body which changes, as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George sa3's, with each government. The audit of accounts should not be left in the hands of auditors appointed by such a board. These accounts should be subject to the scrutiny in every detail, either of the Public Accounts committee of this House or of auditors independently appointed by parliament for the purpose of safeguarding the expenditures made by the people of this country on Montreal harbour, whose money it is and who are merely advancing it on the strength of securities the interest upon which is defrayed and the sinking fund provided out of tolls exacted to a very substantial extent in the final analysis against the products of western Canada that is in the case of the outgoing traffic-and on the manufactured goods and other commodities that come into the harbour of Montreal for shipment to every part of the country. Every pound of freight that goes to the prairies, every bushel of grain that leaves the prairies and goes to the harbour at Montreal, is making a contribution to those facilities and therefore helping to pay the interest on the $12,000,000 we are asked to advance to-night.
For those reasons, considering the paucity of information at the command of the minister, the lack of information, and the necessity of obtaining this information, I am compelled to accord my disinclination to approve of this expenditure this session. I do think
that in the interest of the country as a whole and this parliament in particular, these expenses should be and must be audited or referred to the Public Accounts committee before we conclude to vote money by millions, as we are doing, for this harbour.

I want to associate myself with the suggestion made by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), to this degree at least,, that the accounts of the Montreal harbour board-and I rise for the purpose of adding to that the accounts of the Vancouver harbour board also-should be placed under the control of parliament. I will illustrate the necessity of that, or I will add to the illustrations already given, by pointing out that in the case of my own city, Vancouver, I am confident that there has been some very grave and gross extravagance in the construction of the works there during the last few years. I do not wish at this time to attack the department or the harbour commission of Vancouver, but I say, with equal emphasis to that of my hon. friend Who has just spoken, that these accounts should be subject to the scrutiny of parliament, and I certainly will welcome the motion he mentions for next session. I suggest to him now that he should add to that, "other harbour boards organized similarly to that of Montreal."
I may say, to show to the minister and the hon. members representing the Montreal district that there is no malice in my mind toward that city, that when the Vancouver harbour commission was organized I had to do with it almost entirely; in fact I introduced the bill, or got the government to introduce the bill, and at my own expense had the original bill drafted. I modelled it after the Montreal harbour board scheme, so that I approve of it. I have great respect of the record of the Montreal harbour board and its accomplishments, but that does not, I think, bar us from offering constructive criticism of its actual administration and suggesting a change in that one respect which I think would bring a great deal more confidence to the mind of the public generally. These great public bodies, spending millions of public money-d speak now particularly of the Vancouver and Montreal harbour boards, whose organization is practically identical-should subject themselves to the scrutiny of parliament through the Public Accounts committee, and I believe also through the Auditor General's department. Perhaps it is too late in the session to deal with a matter of this kind.

Montreal Harbour Commission
but I would suggest to the government that between now and next year the department having to do with these two commissions should prepare a careful presentation for the Public Accounts committee of the major capital expenditure in both harbours during the last four or five yiars. I know that in the case of the Vancouver harbour it will be difficult to explain some of the extravagant expenditures, and I may also add this: once there is extravagance in connection with a capital expenditure, that saddles for all time, or for a great many years, on that port the necessity for raising an unnecessary amount of money to pay the annual charges in the way of interest and sinking fund. This in turn is raised by the tolls upon the shipping, and thus the rates are increased beyond what they ought to be, if there is extravagance. Consequently it is very necessary to keep those expenditures down to the lowest possible point.
1 Mr. BENNETT: Would the minister consider this amendment to the bill, which it might be possible to introduce on the third reading:
That the expenditure of the money hereby or heretofore granted shall be subject to audit by an auditor to be appointed by the parliament of Canada and to investigation by the Public Accounts committee of the House of Commons.
I mention that for consideration by the minister, and between now and the third reading of the bill he might be able to agree to it. I am not sure of the exact language which should be used, but that is the sense of what I have in mind.

I am pleased to agree to
the recommendation which has been made by the bon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member 'or Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens): I am sure the harbour commission of Montreal, of Vancouver or elsewhere will have no objection at all to submitting themselves to a more direct control by parliament. We are following the practice that has been established since the corporation was formed, and, so far as they are concerned, I do not see any objection at all to an audit of their books; in fact they have been audited. In the course of last year the Auditor General went to Vancouver and made an audit of the books of the harbour commission. He went to Montreal and made an audit of the books. there. I think at the present time these harbour commissions come under the Audit Act.

Their accounts do not'
come before the Public Accounts committee. Many things are audited, but they never come before the Public Accounts committee of Canada. Things disclosed before the auditor would not come before the House for acceptance by that body.

I think it is a matter of congratulation that the port of Montreal is receiving such a large increase in business, tonnage and receipts. The government have spent $44,000,000 on the harbour and now propose to give them $12,000,000 more, making a total of $56,000,000. The Montreal harbour board had jurisdiction over the channel of the rSver between Montreal and Quebec from 1854 to 1890, when it was transferred to the Department of Public Works. In 1894 the control of the river channel between Montreal and Quebec was transferred to the1 Department of Marine and Fisheries where it remains to-day. I think it is the desire_ of every Canadian that the harbour board shall1 have money to carry on their work. Any remarks I have to make will not be in criticism of the work because every Canadian desires to see this national port grow and progress. On the deep channel from Quebec to Montreal the're was spent in all $44,000,000, which added to the $56,000,000 will make $100,000,000 spent on the Montreal 'harbour and approaches; add to that the million spent on railway terminals and railway facilities, expenditures amounting to perhaps $50,000,000 or $60,000,000 for railway approaches. I think this port should be taken out of politics and managed from the commercial aspect, and the same should apply to Quebec and Vancouver. The minister should consider whether there should n-ot be a nonpolitical board established to manage the affairs of all the federal and national ports, bo that there would not (be a change of board every time there was a change of government, thus making for continuity. If the Canadian National Railway board should be a non-political1 organization, so should our national ports. It is an economic and business question, not a political one. In my opinion, a general act should be passed applying to all these harbour commissions and it should be brought up to date, providing for capital charges, sinking fund, interest and everything else. This board have spent $56,000,000 and they have a sinking fund of one per cent of the loan or only $1,000,000, or one fifty-sixth of the total amount of their capital. This is far too low and it is not proper financing. I do not wish to offer any criticism because I

Montreal Harbour Commission
believe the port of Montreal is going to go ahead by leaps and bound's in the volume of business brought to Canada. I believe every assistance should be given the board to function in a businesslike manner. The present commissioners under the .party system of control are no better or worse than those under the Conservative administration, and I believe they have the interest of the port at heart. I know some of the commissioners and I believe they give a great deal of their time and attention to this work as did their predecessors. In my opinion this great national port should be conducted from the commercial aspect and taken out of politics altogether.
Another feature of the matter that should be dealt with is this. This question was discussed at a 'convention of port authorities when they were here from all over the world from England and other places. Some arrangement should be made for a civic boulevard, park and recreation scheme along this magnificent stretch of river and the island of Montreal in unison with the harbour. I hope they will not make the same mistake that was made in regard to the port of New York, where conditions are somewhat similar to those at Montreal. Recently three commissioners were appointed by the state of New York and three by the state of New Jersey to look after the port of New York. They have jurisdiction over 800 miles of territory around the island on the ocean and rivers. They have found that it is too late to reclaim the water front; that they should have started fifty years ago, and I hope this board will not make the' mistake that has been made in other places but will redeem forever the whole water front. They should construct a proper boulevard and harbour driveways and parks to provide breathing spaces for the working people of the1 great city of Montreal. Some time ago at the convention I discussed this matter with the president and members of the commission and suggested that a harbour survey be made on these lines, not only from the business standpoint but from the standpoint of beautifying the waterfront and affording a breathing space in the near future for the masses of the people of Montreal.
The minister should bring down some better capital financing of this particular project. Certainly a million dollars is not enough for a sinking fund for $56,000,000 of debt, and as regards the interest charges and capital there should be some refunding scheme for this debt. The various loans should have a refunding basis. This money is not a guarantee of bonds; it is a direct .advance of cost up to
$58,000,000 to the board. We should not depend upon the 'harbour board audit or a departmental audit of the accounts of this board. We should have a professional auditor appointed by parliament to audit the work of this and other boards and report to parliament direct, in order to see that the Canadian people have received value for their money. The Toronto commission do not get one cent from this government; all the money they spend is money' guaranteed by the city. All the money spent in that port by the Dominion government since confederation amounts to $8,000,000 although the revenues are from $90,000,000 to $96,000,000 a year. As regards the three ports, Montreal, Quebec, and Vancouver, a general act should be passed and brought up-to-date to provide for a uniform system of audit, a uniform sinking fund, and a uniform method of financing the work, and of refunding and repayment of the loan. The hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) referred the other night to some sales of land, and he read an affidavit. I believe the port on the whole has done very good work under all governments, but we must not forget that it is operating a public trust. I have confidence in the minister and the department but I believe we should have an independent audit made once a year by someone responsible, not to the board, not to the department, but to the high court of parliament.
I notice the operating receipts of the port are increasing very rapidly. Something should be done to prevent the discrimination which has been brought out in this particular debate against the port of Montreal for the benefit of Portland and other ports in the United States. I do not believe the port of Quebec has ever had a chance. It was a seaport before Montreal. In 1854 Montreal was no more a seaport than Hamilton, Belleville, or Port Oolborne on lake Ontario. It was made a seaport by deepening the channel between Quebec and Montreal at an expenditure of nearly $50,000,000. We in Ontario claim that this deep waterway system should be extended to the head of the lakes.
In my opinion Montreal is not what might be called a free port; it cannot be a free port because they have to pay interest and sinking fund but they should try to work up to the time when the port may become a free port. Although Canada receives $4,000,000 in revenue, that is only a small drop in the bucket of what would accrue to Canada if Montreal could be a free, port and attract not a thousand but two thousand ships. The largest ports

I hope the day will come when we shall have a nonpolitical commission in charge of this and other ports. I would like to ask

Is that the policy of the department in conducting investigations under this act? It would seem to be most extraordinary. I remember very well at the time the Hon. Mr. Jones of Woodstock was acting for the accused, and he complained most bitterly that they were not allowed the opportunity to cross-question any witnesses, or to submit any evidence in their own behalf, or to do the things which ordinarily an accused person is allowed to do. I would like to know what is the policy of the department in conducting investigations of this kind. It seems so wholly and absolutely contrary to the principles of law and right and justice. A man accused ought surely to have the chance to see who his accusers are. He surely ought to have the opportunity of cross-questioning witnesses who give evidence, and the opportunity of giving evidence in his own behalf. Then you can have a fair investigation as a result of which you may reach a reasonably proper conclusion. Without that the investigation would be utterly devoid of the merit which an investigation conducted in accordance with the principles of law would have. No one knows at what time some other firm of reputable dealers might be accused of violating the principles of the act, and it seems highly important to know that at least they would be accorded what we would call fair play, an opportunity of cross-questioning witnesses, and of giving evidence in their own behalf. Has the minister read a
decision of the Privy Council on the Industrial Disputes Act which would indicate that legislation with respect to combines is ultra vires of this parliament? I raise the question that the money being voted for this purpose is going to lead nowhere. There is no country in the world where trusts are flourishing like they are in Canada to-day. When the British North America Act was passed there were no such things in Canada as combines, gentlemen's agreements, or interlocking directorates, and under that act matters relating to property and civil rights were confided to the provinces. I venture to say that if an appeal is taken on the Combines Act to the Privy Council a judgment similar to that given in the industrial disputes case will be rendered, on the ground that it conflicts with property and civil rights and employer and employee. The Industrial Disputes Act from cover to cover was ultra vires of this parliament, and the same is true of the act we are now considering. The Privy Council held that the Industrial Disputes Act conflicted with property and civil rights in the provinces, interfered with contracts between employers and employees, and dealt with properties wholly in the provinces. I believe the eight-hour day legislation, except as to day labour on Dominion works, is beyond our competence for the same reasons.
In 1921 we were told that the Conservative party were the creatures of the big interests, and that if the Liberal party were returned
to power they would turn down the combines. "Death to the trusts" was the slogan of the Liberals at that time. But what action did they take when they came into power? They introduced legislation to put an end to the Atlantic combine and an investigation was made into the question which lasted for weeks. But the ocean combine is still doing business and carrying on a land office business at that. In the United States they have the anti-Sherman trust law and they have been carrying it out most effectively. The coal, bread, and sugar combines were dealt with and the Standard Oil Company was brought to book. Judge Landis fined the Standard Oil Company fifty million for breach of the anti-Sherman act. They secured results over there, and they got some measure of control in the regulation of rates. But what control have we got in this 'country.? In 'Canada where we had seventeen banks we have now twelve; various banks have been amalgamated, and we have the manufacturers' trust, the transportation trust, the ocean combine, the bread combine and many other combines. The Liberals said, "We will bring these combines to time if we are continued in power." Did they do so? No. Did they put proper provisions in their charters? No. There is a clause in the Criminal Code with reference to these matters providing for prosecutions of restraints of trade, but how many prosecutions have taken place under that provision in the code? None. How many investigations have they held under the Combines Act? There has been one prosecution out at the coast, the fruit case, but if this case was taken over to the Privy Council I believe the Combines Act would be declared ultra vires. I hope it will be a long Defferred Day in Canada when we will abolish appeals to that greatest of courts, tire Privy Council.	I
am not satisfied with the details of this vote this year or last year. There has been a prosecution of some fruit men, and results of the prosecution went into the lawyers' pockets. That is all the result. More mergers have been consummated under the present government than were ever formed in Canada before. A prosecution of the milk combine was started in Toronto and the judge would not accept the bill of indictment. The milk dealers sat down at a table and arranged it among themselves. They said, "You sell here" and to another man, "You sell there", and so on, and in effect they agreed to enhance prices. One would ask, "What are you selling for", and the other man would tell him, and they all agreed and said, "We will all sell at the same price". They sat down around the
Sppply-Labour

table and fixed the prices, and of course in that way those prices were enhanced. A prosecution was attempted; an. application was made. I think before Mr. Justice Kelly, and he would not accept the bill of indictment on the crown's advice in 1921.
A little while later, in 1923, the Minister of Labour in 1923, brought down a measure which was passed in this House. Of all the machinery that was ever coined or invented by a government that was the most wonderful. It was a dream; it should have been placed in the Victoria Museum, to show to future generations the activity of the present government in prosecuting combines. What do they require to do? If they believe a combine exists under the act they send a man up to see some of the officials of the Labour department. I would not wish to criticize the young Minister of Labour; my criticism does not relate to him but to the act. You have to get at headquarters to destroy the combine. This act is due to the manner in which our charter, the British North America Act, has been framed. Those who drafted the act had not in mind special agreements, interlocking directors, (gentlemen's agreements and lawyers' agreements. I do not believe it is possible that the act will come within the four corners of section 92 of the British North America Act. they have a different constitution in the United States. I fail to see that any useful purpose will be served by spending $30,000 and I venture to say that if the minister got the opinion of the Justice department on this particular act he would find that it is ultra vires for the same reason that the Industrial Disputes Act was declared ultra vires.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
In connection with disputes in the coal fields of British Columbia, Alberta and eastern Canada, these men made investigations and gave to that matter close attention with very beneficial results. Perhaps I could give some cases with which my hon. friend would be familiar. I find on reference to the Annual Report of the Department that Mr. Harrison in the Vancouver office was successful in securing an adjustment of wages and rates affecting workmen employed on the construction of the subway at Edmonton which was being built under agreement between the municipality and the Canadian National Railways. The dispute had previously led to a strike of several weeks' duration in mid-winter and had been the subject of protracted discussion between the authorities concerned and the workmen's representatives. Mr. Compton, resident fair wage officer in Toronto, spent a great deal of his time during the winter in connection with labour questions arising on contracts for the Welland ship canal, which are dealt with in the report of the Department of Labour. Thomas Bertrand, resident fair wage officer in Montreal, investigated
eleven industrial disputes in the year, involving 258 employers and 3,640 employees. Assistance was rendered wherever possible in securing working agreements between the parties affected. In several instances mediation through the departmental officer was instrumental in preventing threatened interruption of work.
Under what authority are those men working? Is it purely a voluntary effort on their part, or have they any statutory authority behind the work they are doing?

As regards conciliation

Perhaps it is hardly fair to criticize a new minister, but I should like to say a few words in regard to the department and the way in which it has been conducted in the last few years. It seems to me that the previous minister had as his object very largely to cut down wherever he could, to make all sorts of small economies involving the curtailment of the real work which ought to be done by a department of this character. Anyone who has had anything to do with the publications of the Department of Labour in the United States will know how much more extensive the work carried on by that department is than has ever been attempted by our department in Canada. Years ago when I had to make some investigations in connection with the interprovincial bureau of which I had charge in the west, I found that I could go to the United States bureaux and obtain very full information with regard to almost any phase of labour conditions, but with regard to Canada the situation was almost hopeless. There were very few investigations; we had contented ourselves with reports of studies which had been made in other places. If this Department of Labour is going to take any real part in the solution of the industrial problems of this country, we ought to have a staff of well-equipped investigators continually making researches and studies of various kinds. I can not but contrast this department, we will say, with the Department of Agriculture, where various experiments with regard to diseases and the welfare of animal and plant life are carried on on a most extensive scale. We have in connection with our industries theihselves an industrial research council which is doing very fine work in making researches and experimentations along various lines. If it is of so great importance for us to experiment with regard to industries or to investigate the whole situation
Sppply-Labour

with regard to plant or animal life, I cannot see why we should not pay a little more attention to the various conditions which affect the labouring population of this country. We have for example our casual labourers drifting about from one part of this country to another. Who knows anything about them? Who knows the reason for their movement? Who is making any attempt whatever to stabilize the labour market. It is all very well, as we note in the next item, to have a department devoted to co-ordinating the employment bureaux, but we shall have to go a great deal further than that. Why should not someone make an examination, for example, into the question of seasonal labour? Undoubtedly in this northern country we must always face the problem of seasonal work. We cannot change our climate. We require a very much larger force of labour in the summer than we do in the winter months and we are content smiply to turn these labouring people out when the fall and the freeze-up come, and allow them to shift for themselves. As individuals they cannot do very much, but if there was a department which was alive to the situation there would be all sorts of studies going on as to how we could dovetail certain types of summer work into certain types of winter work which ought to be developed in this country. According to recent magazine articles, even our friend Henry Ford, who is so versatile, is turning his attention to the employment of some of the factory workers on the farms. At times when factories are slack, the workers can pass to the farms where their services are required. I give that just in passing as a possibility that might be developed by an alert and capable labour department.
There are one or two specific matters that I should like to mention. In the publication to which the minister has made reference we have tables given us as to the cost of living. In connection with our investigations on the minimum wage question before the committee this year we found that the officers of the department had investigated only part of the cost of living; that is, a certain minimum for food, clothing and shelter is recorded, but nothing whatever is said as to the other items which must enter into the matter if a family is to maintain a reasonable standard of living as we understand it. It seems to me that the present way of stating the living costs gives us a very false impression. Frequently this family budget is taken as a basis for estimating certain wage schedules; yet on the face of it, and according to the testimony of officers of the department, it does not really
[Mr. Woodsworth.J
represent the cost that is necessary in order to maintain a family. I would suggest to the minister that those statements be changed and that provision be made for other items that are necessary if a workman is to maintain anything like a decent standard of living.
We have the Labour Gazette, and if I am rightly informed as supplemental to the gazette, there is a publication called Labour Organization of Canada, of which the fifteenth annual report contains a great deal of valuable information. I should like to call the attention of the minister to the very large space given to the discussion of certain aspects of labour that really are not very prominent. Among the regular labour organizations, for example, I find one whole section devoted to revolutionary labour societies, such as the Red International of labour unions, the Communist Party of Canada, and so forth. Some pages of this, I notice, were reproduced in Toronto Saturday Night practically in toto, and already they have been quoted extensively in this House. I submit that we have a right to expect the department to give us a somewhat more balanced account of labour as it really exists. I know there are some people who are very much afraid of the "red menace." I remember two or three years ago the students of Toronto University invented a new yell. Some of the graduates of universities will understand what a college yell is, and this one ran something- like this:
Revolution!, Riot! Blood and gore!!
Down with the capitalist evermore!
One! Two! Three!
Who are we?
B-O-iL-IS-H-E-V-I-K-I! !
That song was actually reported to the police of Toronto, and I cannot see how it possibly escaped being recorded in this document as one indication of red tendencies prevailing among the students of our universities.
Mr. McG'IBBON: Will the hon. member tell us when that was adopted as the college yell of Toronto university?
I heard it sung by some of the students of that university.
That is not what the hon. member said.
I said they discovered or invented that yell.
You said they adopted it.

In this document, which covers the whole country and which is used as a basis for the investigation of labour affairs in Canada, we have one section devoted to labour in politics, and again great prominence is given to a communist organization. I am rather jealous of this because I belong to another organization which at election time is more or less opposed by the communists. It is outrageous.
Out-page-us.

It seems to me there is a little bias evident in some other respects in this document. I do not know what officer is responsible for it. A list is given of the labour papers in Canada, among which I notice the Weekly News of Winnipeg, a small publication in which, as it happens, I am interested, inasmuch as it prints most of what I write. But there is another paper much older and with a very much wider circulation, the One Big Union Bulletin, which is not even mentioned in this official list of labour organs in this country. The minister just now calls my attention to the fact that the information that the official paper of the One Big Union is the O.B.U. Bulletin and is published in Winnipeg is given on another page. It is not included in the list of labour papers. This may be an oversight, but I suggest that where a little paper, such as the one in which I am personally interested, is included-and I am glad of that fact-this other and more extensively circulated publication should certainly not be omitted, and this omission would seem to indicate either ignorance of the actual labour situation or a prejudice against particular labour unions. I call attention to these facts not with the idea of denouncing the department, but rather with a view to encouraging a little more accuracy and a somewhat more extensive investigation
in dealing with the labour situation in Canada. I am convinced that there would be much less apprehension of and a great deal less prejudice towards certain sections of the labour movement if that movement were better understood by the large majority of the people.

The hon. member will have all the time he wishes to make his reply. As I say, he prides himself upon being a representative of labour in this House and on every occasion that offers he informs us that his one object in life is to help the labouring man. Now, the hon. gentleman has been in this House for four or five sessions, and I ask him, through you, Mr. Chairman, what he has ever done or advocated during that time to help the cause of the labouring men of Canada. As a matter of fact, he has supported policies that have driven tens of thousands of our workingmen from their jobs and many of us to-day are representing constituencies that have been so affected. It is time, Sir, that those who advocate the rights of our labouring men put forward something constructive to help those men earn their daily bread and maintain their families. Mr. Chairman,
while the matter I am about to mention perhaps does not come under this item, yet when we were discussing it last year the Minister of Justice promised to give it his attention. Mr. Chairman, to revert for a moment to the question I asked the minister before, is there any statutory author-
ity for these investigators or conciliators to act in adjusting disputes between employers and employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Section 12 provides for
the disseminating of accurate statistical and other information relating to conditions of labour, the collecting and digesting of all information possible and putting it into suitable form so as to show the conditions of labour, and the conducting of inquiries into important industrial questions upon which adequate information may not be available, and so on. There is no doubt that under this section and sections 6, 7 and 9, there is ample power to prevent disputes by conciliation.

The minister misunderstands my question entirely. I was not referring to the collection of information with regard to the conditions of employment generally; that is purely a statistical matter. His answer leads me to the conclusion that in regard to this item it is not a question of conciliation between employers and employees, but that it deals merely with the collecting of information as to existing conditions. There was a time when the department did real valuable service in effecting conciliation between employers and employees in genuine disputes, but through precipitate action taken a few years ago the department has been placed in a position that to my mind now renders it impotent in cases of that character. My own view is that unless the Department of Labour or the government responsible for the department undertakes to re-establish the Conciliation Act, which would more properly come under item 238-Industrial Disputes Investigation Act-the Department of Labour might just as well go out of existence, because all we are getting from it now is merely a matter of statistics. In that connection may I say that this is one of the departments that creates the multiplicity of statistics that have to be furnished where two or three sets of the same statistics are furnished to different departments of the government. If this whole work were turned over to the chief statistician, I am confident that it would be done much better, and all the information we now get would be available.
So far as the work for which the Department of Labour was really designed, .is concerned, namely, to be the medium through which and by which disputes between employers and employees could be conciliated, the situation now is that the department is doing nothing of that character whatever. If there is anything to which a Minister of

Supply-Labour
Labour might direct, his attention, it is I think to bring about a common understanding between the federal and provincial authorities by which there could be a federal measure of genuine conciliation, something of the nature of the Industrial Disputes Act, which has been declared ultra vires of this parliament, because the number of disputes that will arise between employers and employees that cannot be dealt with by provincial authority is very great. As a matter of fact having had some little experience on both sides of the question, I would say that the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act as it previously existed, and as it was previously carried out, was one of the best acts this country ever had. Surely there should be some way by which the federal and provincial governments could get together and reach the point where the federal department could be given authority to carry on as they did before. As it is now, when you talk about conciliation or about the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act you are talking about something that in reality does not exist, because the so-called investigators have no legal authority whatsoever to intervene in a dispute between an employer and his employees.

The minister referred to
